Hopeful Bertie : "Blue Beard." HUSBAND: "Have you got one of your large, homemade cakes handy, Bella!" Wife (delighted to think her cake is appreciated) : "Yes, dear. I'll cut you off a nice ti ick slice." Husband: "No, don't cut it. I want it to chop some wood !"

Qsbi, eyed the insect very atten- tively. At last he saw him alight on his =woes nose, then immediately fly off. " Ah," exclaimed the negro, "me glad to see you burn your foot !"

ELOQUENT SILENCE.—He: "I am going to make you a present of two bracelets for your birthday. Which do you prefer—silver or gold?" Sha is silent. He: "Well, which do you want?" Still silence. He: "Why don't you answer? I ask you which do you prefer—silver or gold ?" She: "Don't you know, you stupid, that speech is silver, and silence gold ?"

HITTEW THE NAIL ON THE HEAD. —A man was complaining to sonic bystanders that he did not know what was the matter with his horses. He had tried everything he could hear of—condition powder, and all other specifics—but to no purpose. They would not improve the flesh. A stable-boy cf Irish extraction, Whose sympathies were aroused by the story, ceinprehended the situation, and modestly asked: "Did you iver try corn?"

AN INGENIOUS EXCUSE. —A physician received late one evening a note .from three of his fellow practioners : "'Please step over to the club, and join us at a rubber of whist." "Etnelie, dear," he said to his wife, "here I am called away again. It appears to be a difficult case—there are three other doctors on the spot already." An intolerable bore having talked a friend .nearly out of his senses, finally struck eat on " the oyster," which he called "one of the most remark- able -specimens of creative wisdom extant," when his friend interrupted him, and "closed the debate" with the exclamation, "The oyster? Ah, yes; the oyster is a glorious fellow, lie always knows when to shut up 1"

When you have succeened in doing this, you can then go ahead with perpetual motion with some prospect of success."

The patient, turning a little pale, exclaimed, "Lord, air ! I hope there is no danger !" " Yes, indeed, there is," replied the surgeon ; "for if the fellow doesn't use his heels, the wound will heal before he returns."

THE ANTIQUARY IN ERROR. —A famous anti- quary—an enthusiast in the search for Roman antiquities—was travelling through England, when he bard that on a certain lull there was a stile calel "Ci.esar's Stile." " Just so," thought the antiquary. "Such a road, mentioned in An o- ninus, passed near here, and the traditional name of this stile confirms me in the opinion that there was a Roman camp on this spot." Whilst he was surveying the prospect a peasant earns up, whom the antiquary addressed : " rhey call this Ciesar's Stile, do they not ? ' " Ess, zur," said the man. "They call it $33 after poor out Bob Cresar, tie ,earpenter. I helped him to make it when I was a boy." MR. SUALLTALK, having been introduced to Miss Dittotoo, says " Very nice assemblage." Very ; and quite literary, too." " Very. on are fond of literature, I presume?" "Au, very! I dote on it." "You like ,!-iliakespeare, I dare- " Aim, very nuech ! Do you?" " Very loud of him; I like Burns, too." "So do ; very much indeed." "Do you • like Goldsmith ?" "Very, very much. Do you like Byron?" " Think he's grand. Do you like Pope?" "Oh, yes ; very much. Do you like Shelley?" "Oh, yes; he's good. Tell you a good writer." " Who?" "Milton." "Yes, he's very good indeed." Afterwards Mr. Smalltalk, in speaking of the young lady, says that she is wonderfully well read ; and she, in speaking of him, says, " Oh ! he has read almost everything, I think." div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
Society circles are much concerned just now about the Christian name that is to be given to the Duke of York's son. Current report says that Albert Henry will be finally decided upon.

It is now beycnd dcubt that some of the mem- bers of the Opposition have within the last week or two received strong warnings from their election agents in regard to the hostility displayed on the Unionist benches towards the Budget. These warn- ings have been to the effect that obstruction to the Finance Bill is unpopular and will cost the mem- bers concerned a good many votes at the general election. Curiously enough, these indications of popular feeling seem to have become more pro- nounced since the debates on the whislcy and beer duty began than they were during the discussion on the estate duty clauses, which the Government have all along considered to be thetnore popular part of their measure. This, however, may be because the points at issue are better understood. In any ease, the fact that there have been such warnings is no longer concealed, and they have come from very different parts of the country,though mostly, I believe, from the large towns. The cases which have come to my knowledge are those of Conser- vative members, but many Liberal Unionists must, I should fancy, have "heard from" their consti- tuents.

The arrival of the Home Secretary at White Lodge some time before the latest Royal birth took place is in accordance with a precedent which has existed ever since the time of James 11., which requires that one of the Secretaries of State, an other high officials, shall be present on these occasions. The, rule had its, origin in the "warming pan" story. When the Queen bore a son to the last of the Stuart kings—the son who became the elder Pretender—it was long and widely believed that the child was :-upposititious. No one of any authority now holds that there was any foundation for this story of the introduction of a child in the warming-pan; but still, to prevent the revival of such a report in the case of children of the Royal line, certain officials of high position are always summoned on such occasions.

Mr. Robert Wallace, M.P., purposes starting ear'y in the autumn on an extended lecturing tour in the United S•ates and Canada. His subjects are varied and interesting, from ' "Robert Burns, Poet and Philosfipber," to "Confessions of a Jack of all Trades." Mr. Wallace is already aesured of a hearty welcome. •

Lord Randolph Churchill will not, during his journey round the world, act as a special correspon- dent of an English newspaper, as he did when he visited South Africa. lie has, however, accepted an engagement to write four articles for a Paris journal.

The cycle world here is in a state of very con-, siderable excitement over toe extraordinary per- formances on the Herne Hill track of the Sou' 1-` Wales lad whose record cutting in all directions w 11 ut our best cyclists to a new trial of their power- I n the bundled miles race of the Surrey Btet Club be had siktinst him some of the very best itteA known, men of high reputation and gr t . nerience in long-distance contests. Nevetthe e. ue broke the highest known 100 mile record by 1, n oainutes ; and, what is more, he broke every exist- ng record above 49 miles. But for a strong and adverse wind the 100. mile record would have been broken by a still larger figure. His introduction to the London racing -world is due to Linton, the holder till the present of highest 100-mile ;recce, who now finds his own honours taken from him. [he new hero, Michael by name, is only 17 years of age, and is a butcher near Cardiff, but there 'siLl now be a competition for his services amoui.:. be great manufacturing firms, who will try to adver- tise their machines by means of his great riding powers.

There was a large muster of the political econom- ists of the National Liberal Club on Wednesday night, to hear 'M. Yves Guyot's paper on • "The die- tribution ot real property in France." in the course of the paper, which was full of interesting Statistics the author pointed out that eight out of every ten persons in France possessed real property, and that the large properties only amounted to some 23 per cent. of the whole. With regard to houses, nearly 90 per cent. were under £5 rental. Ile also showed hat the number of single proprietors in France had steadily increased since 1789; that, in conse- quence, the number of agricultural labourers had iessened ; and he also observed that there was a distinct tendency towards a lessening of the met, or taxes on land. Mr. Stansfield, Ml'., who pre- sided, pointed out in closing the discussion that the whole drift of the valuable paper *as in favour 01 he system of peasant proprietorship,and he looked forward to the near future when Eugland, with due regard to the different national conditions,"'woulu eidvance in the same direction. lie felt sure that recent changes in local government were an import- ant step in this direction. Previously Dr. Hunter, 31.1)., emphasised the inadequacy of English real property statistics, saying that similar facts with regard to England did not exist; while Mr. Joseph Arch, whose speech was warmly received, iiius. crated from hi 3 own personal experience the diffi- euly in former years of obtaining small holdings. Young men had now, however, holdings which I hey could themselves cultivate, and therelore they had no desire whatever to increase the crowds of unemployed in London and other large COMM

One would have expected that the last to be shadowed by detectives would have been Louise But she cannot move about without there oeing a detective watching her in front cud an ther oehind. It is not to protect her life that this vigil- ance Is exercised, but to observe her movements and any possible communiCations with other revolu- , 'unary spirits. The recrudescence of Anarchist activity has made the detective department of the. police in London, as everywhere else, unusually observant, and there is probably not an Anarchist of any note in the metropolis whose movements are, not known to the police. But the rapidly-age - ing Louise Michel, woo is plAying the part ot French philanthropist in London, being dogged and watched, crowns all the efforts of the detective department.

Sir W. Harcourt's little holiday at Illalwood is another indication that the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer has become weary of the turmoil and was- fare of the House of Commons, and longs for seclu- sion and rest. Ile will find both in the charming solitude of the New Forest, perhaps to his own great relief, but to the irreparable bss of the Liberal party, whenever he lays down his harness and leaves the arena of political strife. The splen- did budget which he has just piloted through the [louse of Commons has earned for him the lasting gratitude of all Liberals, and there is no wonder (mat his political friends in Parliament talk of cele- brating his great services by entertaining him at dinner in reccgnition of his historical achievement. For it is nothing short of a financial revolution that se has begun, and future Chancellors of the Es- chequer will work upon the lines of it, and develop its principles for the accomplishment of results which only a few dream of at present. In the principles which are to be found asserted in Sir William's Budget lies the whole future of demo- cultic finance. When democracy becomes strong enough, it will find itself in possession of a weapon which it can use for carrying out almost, every object ever dreamed of by the most revolutionary mind.

It may be a pleasing and graceful whim that leads the Royal Family to have all their babies baptised with water brought from the Jordan, and one might look upon the liquid with profound awe and veneration if it were precisely the same water that was in the river 1800 years ago. But it may be taken as perfectly certain that even i. the Dead ea itself there is not a single drop of water which was in it at that distant date ; and what particular advantage there is in sending all the way to the Jordan for water with which to christen the young Prince, in consequence of her Majesty's own supply hallug become exhausted, is not apparent to a matter-of-fact mind. llowever, if not too scientifi- cally examined, it possesses a certain glamour of interest, but, looking to Oriental habits, I hope her Majesty will have it duly filtered and well boiled before silo allows it to be used for its sacred pur- pose.

MY DEAREST NELLIE, Plain skirts are still largely worn, and a new style of trimming consists ot stripes, placed length- ways on either side of the front, and sometimes repeated on either side of the back. Velvet, pas- sementerie, or moire ribbon is used in this style; or lines of coloured silk, covered lace insertion, or even with piece guipure, and outlined with n Irrow passementerie. [here are many novelties in fronts and waiscoats for opzn coats, but the newest are distinguished by a wide, full bow at the neck. A front of spotted Hose consists of lengthway folds of the single-width material brought up to the neck, and finishing with a full bow at the throat. Another forms a graduated cascade of accordion- pleated chiffon, the ends joined at the neck, and spread on either side to imitate a bow. Black is undoubtedly the most useful of all gowns where it Is required for widely diverse occasions and with a couple of good black tops, and one black skirt and one or two of neutral colouring, it is possible to vary the toilette immensely, and yet be always well and smartly attired. A particularly effective costume if made of fancy silk is used in combina- tion with plain material, or even a plain silk of contrasting colour.

When the Empress Eugenie had hr greatest vogue as a beauty the distinguishing feature of her good looks was her pure and regular profile. This has survived the disfiguring action of years. and gained in, refihement, so that though Eugenie is now a faded and gfey-haired lady her face is still a most interesting one. The baby at White'Lodge, which has been the theme of s:4 many newspaper chroniclings, bulletins, and com- ments, was weighed at his birth, and turned the scale at eleven pounds. This was a quite satisfactory result. He is fed from the bottleJ, and is. said to be making extremely good progress. It is generally believed that, when his mother is auffiliently recovered to go to the country she will spend some time in the. Isle of Wight, in anticipation of which, as was announced some time ago, a residence is being prepared by the Queen for her reception. She is said to have a desire to.go later on to the east coast of Kent, but other preferences may arise to alter that iateution.

Moths in Carpets. Moths can be successfully removed from carpets in the following manner: . Wring a coarse towel out of clear water; spread it smoothly on the carpet, iron it dry with a good hot iron, repeating the operation wherever the moths are supposed to be. There is no need to press hard, and the colour of the carpet will not he injured, as the moths are destroyed by the beat and steam.

' Eggs and Milk for Children. Eggs are especially desirable for children, and the youthful frame finds in them everything necessary for its growth. A puny delicate child, td whom all' kinds of food seem repulsive, will often relish raw egg and milk, and gain health and strength therefrom. Every morn- ing, as soon as the little one is taken up, the mother should beat one egg thoroughly with a teaspoonful of castor sugar, and mix with it a pint of milk. A cupful of this should be taken in the morning, and the remain- der for early lunch.

A hat, extremely pretty in shape, and particu- larly successful in colouring, is of black guipure on ailk poppies, mauve and pale creamy yellow, while the gracefully arranged bow is of shot yellow and mauve ribbon. Another stylish hat in auk- coloured chip, the brim being veiled in cream guipure on black jet, is trimmed with pale blue feathers and apricot roses. A third hat is in black drawn net edged with jet, with full torquoise velvet crown. It is trimmed with a soft plume of black feathers, a bow of black moire ribbon, and apricot roses.

it is more clo-sely fitting to the wait than a- old, and is kept down by an inside belt. The style has Eve seams, and each front has a dart. A fashionable garment is the tight-fitting, sleeveless jacket of rnoird nacre and plush, with handacur ieLted belt,

The big moire cravat has been succeeded by huge tulle bows and very full box-pleated ruffs of white net, chiffon (plain and edged with tiny fluffy feathers) or crepe de chine; these latter, which are made up on a foundation of narrow ribbon, being particularly becoming to people whose throats are unduly long and thin. Very large vandyked collars of coarse cream or ecru lace, which are dubbed Cromwell collars, are much in vogue and make a pretty finish to a plain black gown, especially if attached to a deep folded neck-band of bright-coloured velvet. White or very pale grey gloves stitched with black are worn for smart occasions, while, for every day use, black with white sewing are fashionable. An atttempt has been made to bring in gloves trimmed round the wrists with lace, but they are not considered "good style," and will probably soon disappear. tackles on belts—moiré ribbon is all prevailing for these—are either long and narrow, or almost square, and those of paste or cut steel are most popular. Worked curtains are becoming increasingly popu- lar, and a good many novelties have been brought out this season. Very pretty curtains—long or short—are made of a soft cream cotton canvas, worked with a border in coarse ingrain cotton, the centre of the curtain being dotted all over with stiff sprays of flowers, stars, or crosses worked in the same way, long, straight stitches set closely side by side alone used for the whole of the em- broidery (which, by the way, is usually sold under the name of Norwegian-work), and the curtains are often finished along the edge with a narrow hem stitching. Coloured linen, which, with care, washes excellently, is a gocd deal used for window draperies, and a very pretty, as well as useful, pair of bedroom curtains may be made of pale apple. green linen embroidered with monster daisies worked in yellow and white flax, and a room with a pink and white paper, pale green paint, and curtains such as l have suggested, with toilet slips, &c., to match, would have a very dainty appear- ance indeed.
Yours lovingly, JENNIF.

The Queen of Sian has the smallest foot of any titled I THE DOUBLE LIFE • person in the world. She wears one and a half in! Oa, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. boots. The salary of the infant King of Spain is one hundred By the Author of "DABIEWOOD." and fifty thousand pounds. A story is current regarding a gentleman who recently received an invitation to dinner at Marlborough House. He did not know what costume he ought to appear in, so sent a quiet note to the private secretary. Sir Francis Knollys replied that "as no ladies are to be present trousers may be worn." This sounds startling t and might furnish an American journalist with a text tor an imaginative article on the manners and customs of Encrb- lish royalty. The simple explanation of the somewhat dubious message is that as a rule knee breeches are worn with evening dress at Marlborough House. The personal outfit of the seven-days'-old baby has been a matter of much consideration to its two grand- mothers—the Princess of Wales and the Duchess ofTeck. They have, however,managed to secure clothing which, judging from the descriptions given of it, is of a sump- tuous not to say a regal character. There is to me this one satisfactory feature about the business, and that is that wherever possible materials and trimmings of Brit- ish manufacture have been used, the lawn being Irish, the lace Northamptonshire as well as Irish, and the satin woven at, Spitalfields. Everything is of snowy white- ness, and the fineness of the sewing is admirable. In such matters as these stitchery' becomes a work of art, so minute in its character. The small points with which some of the bands are embroidered and the beading that embellishes some of the tiny garments show an exqui- site neatness and finish.
CHAPTER XX. A BIT OF MASQUERADING.

The marquis leaned back in his chair, his large, grand head strongly displayed against its crim- son cushions, his massive, rugged features lighted up with an expression of interest which they had not known • years. His old look of cynicism and misantl,—py was scarcely apparent, and he had resumed, with his evening coat, his old- school air of gallant courtliness, which gave him the aspect of a French nobleman of the ancient regime. It was evident that Giralda had had al- ready a humanising effect upon him. The disguised Lady Beatrice arose at his en- trance, and Giralda said, in a tremulous voice: "Mamma, this is my new friend, of whom I have told you. Lord Trevelyan of Trevelyan Park, in Giamorgaushire. My ford, this is my mother, the Countess of Arevalo." The marquis bowed in courtly style, and her ladyship inclined her head, and, in obedience to his request, sank into the arm-chair opposite him, moving it a little distance into the shadow. "I beg your ladyship to be kind enough to ex- cuse my rising," said the marquis politely, "but lam a martyr to the gout. am a great sufferer— Ah ! that wretch Wigby I" he exclaimed, his old testiness rising to the surface, as he became deathly pale from a sudden twinge in h!s foot. "The old scoundrel! I beg your pardon, madam. You have never had the gout. The unprincipled villain has placed my chairs too near each other. Oh dear I"

He strove to catch at the ball pull, but Giralda sprang forward and moved the offending chair with a gentleness that surprised him. The fur- rows in his brows vanished, and a look of grate- ful relief replaced his expression of pain. "Thank you, my dear," he said simply. "I am quite easy now. Your ladyship," he added, with a resumption of his courtliness, "is no doubt sur- prised to find your little runaway in my care. You must have been very anxious about her." "I was indeed," replied the so-called countess in clear but disguised tones. "She has told me of your great kindness to her, and I cannot suffi- ciently thank your lordship for your interest in the child. I shudder when I think what might 1 have been her fate had she gone to anybody but you." "So do I," declared the marquis frankly. "The I world is a bad place for a young creatin e like Gi- ralda, so innocent and so beautiful. lam an Old man, madam, of seventy-five—old enough to be the child's grandfather, as I wish I was in good truth. My gray hairs and my well-known char- acter must speak or me." And he touched the thick gray curls that clustered close about his massive head, as if he were proud of them. "I am familiar with the name and reputation of Lord Trevelyan," said her ladyship courteously.. " Humph I Then no doubt you have heard little , in my favour," said the marquis. "People call me miserly because I spend little. I allow them to do so rather than to take the trouble to correct their notion. The truth is, Countess, all that a sensible person wants in this world--and all that he gets, too—is his food, clothing and lodging. I My tastes are simple, and I do not care to be at the bother of running about to buy things I don't I want. As to my residence, people complain that it is out of repair, and that its roof leaks. What if it is so? If I don't complain who live there, why should they to whom I would not give shel- ter ? Why should I incommode myself and have my life harassed out by a lot of masons, carpen- ters, upholsterers, and so on, just for the purpose of having people praise me? I ha eno 9liildren to thank me for my trouble; and if my nephew wants to alter the house when he comes into pos- session, why, I sha'n't hinder him." "Your reasoning is certainly unique," said the countess, smiling. "You are a philosopher." "Yes, madam, I .believe I am," declared Lord Trevelyan, with emphatic earnestness. "I hope I have made plain to you that I do not merit the epithet of miserly ' which society applies to me. You have heard that in temper I am a perfect Herod—a cruel, testy, irritable old wretch, with a hard heart and a hard tongue. I plead guilty to that charge. But, Countess," he added, his eyes growing strangely earnest, "you never heard that I wronged a human being. lam harsh, but I 'never wronged a man, woman, or child—never! I never corrupted any one. I have all ay life, in all any dealings with every one, been the incarnation of justice—stern, unyielding, if you will, but still justice ! " "It is well to be just in all things," said the countess, gently, "but in justice we should re- member mercy ! " The rugged face of the marquis darkened a lit- ' tle at this suggestion, but the cloud cleared away almost instantly. "I could be merciful to anything but hypocrisy and studied deceit and ingratitude !" he said, in a stern, hard voice, as if old memories were assert- ting themselves in his soul. "I beg your pardon, Countess," he added, forcing a laugh. "I should display all my best traits to-day, for I want to ask. a favour of you."

A favour Of me ?" questioned her ladyship. "Yes, madam. I told you that I had a hard heart. I thought until lately that it was harder than granite. Your daughter has proved to me that it has a soft spot in it. I love your child. Will you give her to me ?" The Lady Beatrice started in sudden amaze, and caught Giralda's trembling hand in her own. "You love my child ?" she said, in a tremulous voice.

"Do not mistake me, Countess !" cried the old nobleman, earnestly. "I do not love her as young men love when they woo. Your daughter seems to me a child—a bright, lovely, pure child. I am old enough to be her grandfather, as I said before. I am a lonely old man. I have but One relative in the world, and he cares nothing for me. Your little girl seems to feel an affection for me. I love her with a love such as I might have given my own child, had I had one. I want to adopt her !"

"You have known her so short a time, my lord," suggested the countess, placing her ungloved hand upon the dusky ripples crowning her darling's head, and smoothing them softly. "Madam, I am obliged to be a short time in forming my friendships now," returned the old marquis, bitterly. "I may not have many years in which to cultivate friendships of slow growth. There ! you see that I am irritable, as I said. Forgive me, and seal my pardon with your con- sent to my prayer. I will leave your daughter a haodsome fortune, and will make my will to that effect at the earliest possible hour to-morrow morn- ing. I possess a large sum of money—the fruit of years of saving from my immense income. That money, with slime freeholfl property, I will be- queath to Giralda. And all I ask in return is her society at the Park. She may visit you and her home as often as you wish—she shall have every privilege, as if she were really my granddaughter —s, rvants, equipage, company, dress. I shall be amply repaid by feeling that there is some one in the world who loves fne and rejoices that I live !"

He regarded the countess eagerly. Her lady- ship affected to hesitate. "Ciralda has told me that you are an actress, madam," resumed Lord Trevelyan, after a brief pause, "and that she desired to relieve you of the burden of her support. I will gratify all your motherly ambitimis for her. I promise to make her happy. You trust me, and want to go with me, do you not my child ?" he added, sud- denly addressing himself to Ciralda, who had seated herself on a low ottoman beside her mother.

"Yes, I want to go I" declared the young girl, earnestly. "I know mamma will consent, my lord," and she looked up fondly into the disguised face of the Lady Beatrice. Still the mother was silent. Perhaps, at the last, she was loth to trust her darling to the difficult path in which she had desired her to tread.

"Giralda should belong to me," said his lord- ship, " if ,for no other reason than that she looks like my family. If I did not know her to be of Spanish parentage, I should believe her a Trevel- yan. She told me that your ladyship is of English birth—a fact which I had forgotten until this, moment, your air being so decidedly foreign. Is It not possible that you are descended from a branch of the Trevelyan family, madam?" Her ladyship replied in the negative. The eyes of the marquis rested on the maiden for a brief space, and then he said, in an altered voice: • "It is possible that her resemblance to my family contributed to interest me in your daugh- ter, Countess. The resemblance is most singular, adel most striking. But there Was something else that drew me to her with cords of steel. Her .eyes, madam !"—and Lord Trevelyan's voice be- ce•lulo low aud broken with 0. strantN emit/04-7

" her eyes! They are like a pair of eyes 1 knev and loved once. They were the sweetest, the frankest, the most fearless, loving eyes that natare ever set in a; boy's head I Giralda's are like them Looking into her eyes I seem to see that innocent boy again—he was innocent then, and I loved ii rn."

He haded his eyes with one large, white hand, and looked away into the fire. There was a pallor oo his face not produced by physical pain, and a continAion about the lips that told of .a stern re- -1,/-,•s,ion of mirging emotions. The tears flooded Giralda's lovely eyes, and she laid her head on her mother's knee and wept aloud.

• TLe disguised Lady Beatrice struggled hard with her pitying grief. All the bitterness and loneliness of a lifetime had been expressed in his isfrrdhli•p's words, and her desire for a reconcilia- tion baween her husband and his uncle became from toat moment a passion. She had known the margins well for many years, but with her he had always been the cynic and misanthrope, deeming her a heartless belle.
As the sound,of Giralda's sobbing broke the still- ness that had fallen upon the inmates of the room, Cle marquis started and turned around, looking at her in _aAonishinent. _

" the little pitying heart," he murmured, a rare sm: le lighting up his grand and ruggedfeatures. "See how she loves me, Countess I She knows that the boy I spoke of but now was a hypocrite, a thief, and an intended murderer 1" and a sudden blaze shot from his eyes like a flame of fire. "It was he who made me what I am. I curse his memory 1" and he hissed the words between sud- dcoly clenched teeth. "If he were alive I would destroy him ." and an awful look of hatred trans- figured his face. "But he is dead. Thank heaven, his bones do not rest on British soil! He is dead, and his blue eyes are ashes now!"- and again the strong, hard voice quavered. "In memory of the happy days when I believed him true Et,nd loving, give me your child, Countess. Ile was the only being lever loved till now. I had dreams in those far-off days of the time when I should have his children around me. He was engaged then to a noble and beautiful lady, who hos kept herself single I sometimes think for his sake. They were vain dreams, but I shall think sometimes that they have come true, and that it is his child I love Will you let Giralda ? " "She may go," declared the countess in an un- steady voice.. . .
l'n; marquis's face glowed now with a great joy. He had set his heart on the adoption of this loving, lovely creature, and he was overjoyed at his success when he had begun to anticipate failure.
He reached out his hand to the countess, grasp- ing lux delicate member with an iron grip, un- conscious that he was exerting in his earnestness an unnecessary amount of strength. _ _ . _ _ _ _ _

" adam,"-he exclaimed, with a solemnity that sprang from trueleeling, "may 'God deal with me as I deal with your child ! I will cherish her as the apple of my eye. My house will be open to Giralcia's relatives whenever they will gratify her or honour me with a visit. And whatever I can do for you and yours Iwill esteem it a favour to be allowed to do."

The countess replied to these warm declarations with a gentle dignity/that won his esteem. "I have a condition to make, my lord," she said, as she withdrew her hand from his grasp. "lb is that you will shield my daughter as care- fully as if she were yours. I told you that I had lie4rd of you. I have heard also that you have a nephew, a dissipated man. I want my child to be shi hied from his notice."

"If Adlowe dares to look too long upon Giralda's face, he shall never be admitted to the Park again while I live !" asserted the old nobleman, with emphasis. "Rot he won't come to the Park. He never used to trouble me with visits, and his late wanderings in the East cannot have made him more agectionate. I will no more permit her to fall In his way than I would give her up to a wild beast. Rest assured, Countess, that she shall never meet him except in my presence, and never then unless by accident." "I have no further conditions to make. I rely entirely upon your honour and your love for Giralda in thus constituting you her guardian," remarked the disguised Lady Beatrice. "Is there any other point to discuss ?" "Would it be necessary for us to call upon the Count Arevalo ?" inquired the marquis. "10. I will inform him ot what I have done. He is a student, and receives no visitors. He recognises my absolute right to provide for our daughter.' "Then there is nothing to detain us in London beyond to-night?" , "Nothing, so far as Giralda is concerned. I cannot come to see her again, my duties detaining me elsewhere. I suppose now .you would like to hear something of the parentage of your young charge," added her ladyship, smiling. "Her father, as she has informed you, no doubt, is the Count Arevalo. Giralda has also informed you, no doubt, that he is a Spaniard of good birth, as his title implies, and of breeding also. I am an English gentlewoman. I cannot make known my .own family name to you. In England, you know, a family considers itself disgraced when one of its members becomes an actress—"

"1 do not wish to know your family name, interposed his lordship, with sincerity and with gallantry. "You carry a certificate of gentle birth in your looks, your air, and your manner. Because I have desired to adopt your lovely child, do not think that I mean to make that an excuse for prying into your private affairs." " bo you not desire to know at what theatre I am engaged " inquired the countess, smiling. " Have you no wish for 'references,' to be assured that my statements are not overdrawn, and that I am just what I appear? "Not so, madam," replied the marquis, who would have been &hocked by her speech had the counzess's tone beea less light and pleasant. ." I am well assured on every point, and perfectly satisfied—more than satisfied.' "Then I need not prolong my stay," said her ladyship, arising. "1 have stolen the time from my duties, and may be missed if I linger. In re- gard to a legal adoption, my lord, it is not neces- sary. Giralda loves you, and will not leave you so long as you love her and desire her presence. Any provision you may make for her I leave to your honour. I beg you to be very tender and gentle with Amer. And now—farewell." She extended her hand to him in adieu.

And then she gathered her daughter in her arms in a final embrace. The partings were very bitter to both. A sense of the perils surrounding them and their loved ones weighed heavily upon both nether and daughter; Giralda bravely restrained her tears and grief, struggling to soothe the fears tintt now a.ssailed oar mother's heart.
The parting was over. The Lady Beatrice turned to depart, hen suddenly the door was thrust open, and Lord Adlowe, gay and insolent in thnueariour, sauntored into the room. (To be continued).

div.head: Windows.
div.p: Windows.

To remove a broken pane' loosen the putty by passing, a lict iron over the putty. To take paint spots off win- dow-panes, rub hard with hot soda-water. To wa ab windows, uF,,e a teaspoonful of ammonia or a little borax to a quart of hot water. After washing with this solu- tion, fins,: in clear water and polish with soft paper. Use a sharp-pointed stick to clean the accumulation s from the corners of the sash. Do not clean windows when the sun shines on them, as they dry before they can be properly polished.

div.head: To Abolish Flies.
div.p: To Abolish Flies.

Flies are useful scavengers, and if they would limit their inroads to places 'where they are needed, thes would do good service. Unfortunately, however, when they once come in force they are a great ' nuisance in even the most cleanly homes. One of the most succef-s- -ful methods in dealing with flies is to hang up srme ht ro or plant which is offensive to them and not offensive to the residents of the house. Sweet clover, which grows plentifully by the roadside, and has a faint, pleasant odour, unobjectionable to anyone not afflicted with hay fever, has the reputation of being abhorred by flies. A few sprays of this plant hung in the parlour, or placed on a tatale will do more work in ridding the room of flies than a dezen fly-traps.

A Royal Cradle. Here is a description of the et'adle' in which the new born Prince reposes at White bodge,Richmond—a des- cription which no doubt many mothers will read with interest. The cradle is a gift from tbe Queen. and it bears an inscription to' the effeet that it was made in 1840 for the Princess Royal and was used for all of Her Majesty's children. It is fitted up with pure white satin and Honiton lace, and as the basinette is itself in white wood, there is no scrap of colour about it. The Queen has also given a s&cond cradle to the Duchess, made of mahogany inlaid with fine gilding. This is fitted up with brocade in delicately pale tones of colour. The bedding provided for both cradles is of the softest and lightest description. The sheets are of Irish lawn, bor- dered with Valenciennes lace, and the blankets are of Pyrenean wool, very white, and weighin; very I.ttle,tht- teiture more nearly resembling eiderdown than fl-innel Two small eiderdown quilts have been provided for the baby's use, one white and one pale pink.

Alr and brilliant assemblage of guests, inelwiing Mr. G:adstone, were staying at the Castle, and before they rntut d the night Dr. Guthrie was asked by the duke to eon - duct family worship." With great pleasure will I conduct it,' said the doctor; but in the Castle of Argyl! we must observe the good old Presbvt(rian form. an begin by singing a Psalm.' It was agraed that a Scotch psalm should be sung to a Scotch tune; but he diffi culty was to find a precentor '—that is, a g nth man or lady who would raise the tune' and lead the sit- ing. After a number of ladies and !gentlemen hail be ,n appealed to, and had declared themselves unfit ft r •h, duty, Mr. Gladstone stepped forward, saying, rise he tune, Dr. Guthrie ; ' aud well did he perform his task."

THE ENDOWMENT OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH. MUNIFICENCE OF MR. LUDWIG MOND.

Mr. Ludwig Mond, a director of the well-known company of Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co., Limited, of Liverpool. and whose alkali works are situated at Winnington, North wich, and Sandbach, in Cheshire, has offered a splendid gift to the Royal Institution, London, which that body on Monday decided to accept. It spot ars that Mr. Mond last year bought the large freehold house No. 2J, Albemarlest., contiguous to the buildings of the Royal Institution, and formerly the residence of the Earl of Albemarle. This house he has resolved to convey in fee simple to the Royal Institution. He further proposes to defray the whole expenses of converting it from its present uses into a laboratory of ehemical and physical research, to be called the Davy- Faraday Research Research Laboratory, and of equipping it with everything needful for the conducting of scientific re- search upon a large scale. In addition to this, he pro- poses to endow the new laboratory first with an income - sufficient to defrayall the expenses of rates, taxes, and maintenances; and, secondly, with a further and of course much larger income sufficient to pay the salaries and incidental expenses of a trained scientific staff, and generally to carry on the work of an institution of this. kind in an adequate and business-like manner. By this generous offer the financial magnitude of which (says the "Times") will be appreciated by all who are conversant with the necessities of a scientific - establishment on so large a scale, Mr. Mond realises an idea which engaged the attention of Faraday and Brande- and the managers of the Royal Institution half a cen- tury ago. Dar. Mond has felt that the need for such a laboratory has become greater and greater since the work of the scientific investigator has become more and more subtle and exact, and in consequence requires instruments of precision and a variety of facilities which a private laboratory can very rarely command,. It has been his desire for many years to found a public laboratorr which shall give to the devotees of pure science, anxious and willing to follow in the footsteps of the illustrious men who have built up the proud edifice of modern science, the facilities necessary for research in chemistry and more particularly in that branch of the science called physical chemistry. He has come to the conclu- sion as the promoters of the scheme of 1843—viz., that such a laboratory would still have the greatest prospect of success under the mgis of the Royal Institution; that, in fact, it would be the consummation of the work which this great institution has been fostering in its own laboratory with such remarkable results by the aid of the eminent men whose services it has always been fortunate enough to procure. The laboratory is to be free to all persons, without distinction of sex or nationality, who, in the opinion of the managers of the Roy al Institution, are fully qualified to undertake scientific investigation, preference • being naturally given to those who have actually done original work.

After providing for all the needs of the Davy-Faradaf Research Laboratory, the house given by Mr. Mond teP the Royal Institution will afford space sufficient to pro- vide a considerable addition to the accommodation of the Royal Instituti®n itself. Such an extension of its premises is particularly needed to make room for its growing library, and also for the chemical laboratory, where the powerful apparatus required for such investi— gations as those so brilliantly carried on by Professor Dewar demand space undreamed of by the chemists oi an earlier generation.

div.head: BALLOON VOYAGES.
div.p: BALLOON VOYAGES.

It is stated in " Cassell's Illustrated History of the Franco-German War," that the two great institutions of the pigeon and the balloon continued to be of marked service to France. But, as the year drew towards its. close, the pigeons were found to be less useful than they had proved in earlier months. They would not fly dur- ing the night; and the December days. were so short that messages were in this way frequently delayed. When the birds were sent from the south of France, it was necessary to convey them a long part of the way by band, and to set them loose at such a distance from Paris • as they could traverse before sunset. If not, they went t. 2 roost wherever they could, and sometimes failed to con- tinue their journey on the following day. The halloons were also liable to accidents but, on the whole, did wonders in keeping up intercommunication. They were for the most part made or strong calico, covered with two or three coatings of linseed oil and oxide of lead. . and inflated with ordinary gas. Some were manufac- tured at the Northern, others at the Orleans, railway station ; and at the former the pieces were sewn together by machinery. One of the most adventurous of these balloon voyages was that of M. Martin, a naval officer from Finisterre, who gave an account of his experience' , to the Bordeaux correspondent of the " Daily News." . M. Martin started from Paris on the Ist December, in a balloon which had been christened the "Jules Favre.' Lie rose at once above the show 6.Di:cis into a stratum of bitter cold air, along which he was borne with great• speed into aw es erly direction. He felt like a man who had been burl, d alive in a vast, dark, chilling vault, be- yond the reach of human sympathy or aid. Presently the stars were obscured by snow-clouds, and it was also found that the instruments used by aeronauts for taking their bearings had got out of order. At four o'clock in the morning, M. Martin and his cOmpanion perceived. water below them, 'which at first they supposed to be the Loire ; but shortly afterwards, seeing a lighthouse and ships, they found they were in the neighbourhood of the sea. [hey were above Belle-Isle, and close to,the western side of it, a... that it was kecessary to descend at once, if they would not be swept away over the Atlantic' The pulley whim opened t,lie escape-valve had been blown out of reach by the fury of their rushing passage through the air; but M. Martin climbed up the ropes, regained the pulley, and released the gas. They now decended with such rapidity as to loose consciousness. The balloon, on nearing the earth, dashed madly about tore off the roof of a house, broke down a wall,and cam into collision With an Nld church. Mr. Martin's come panion was thrown out and seri*usly hurt, and M. Martin himself, on recovering his senses, ,found that some coast guardsmen were holding down the car. Among the persons soon attracted to the spot was M. Armand Trochu, brother of the Governor of Paris. This gentleman had a little property on Belle-Isle, where he • lived with his mother, their in her eighty-fourth year. By a strange coincidence. it was the roof of M. Armand Trochu's house which the "Jules Favre " tore off in kilt wild writhings. The old lady had been praying through— out the night for a sign from heaven that France should ,be saved by her son ; and wh,n, the rafters crashed over ! her head, she exclaimed to her grand-daughter that the ! sign had been given, and that "the Providence of the- King of Prussia' was not alwa)s to prevail.

The attendance at the P.S.A. meeting io Wycliffe Chive!, on Sunday afternoon was not so large as usual, which may be accounted for by the excessively hot w,atli,r which was experienced, and also the holidays. Mr. A. Lang was the chairman, and he delivered a short interesting aJdress on the motto of the society, " One is your master, even Christ, and all ye are brethren." Dr. Brown, if Manchester, delivered the address, in which he arated that he b.lieved it was possible to have a reli- gion without iheologv. For what was religion ? The epistle SI. James said pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father was this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affl'clion,and to keep himself unspotted from the world. That meant that religion was love and polity. The man who had these two things was reli- gion"), no matter what he believed, or thought, no mat- ter how crude his faith, or how limited his understand- But what was theology ? It was the study of God, and the theo!ogian was a man who studied God. He read all that had been written about God, all he liked he took, atni left the rest. Theology was only of value in Si far a- it helped them to get more and more of the true r, I.gion which was pure and undefiled, or as it helped t*,ein to keep their lives more honourableP make them more gentle and affrctionate in their every-day life. The speaker illustrated his subject by quoting the ry,rablf, ,;f the Good Samaritan. The soloist was Miss K•iit, who sang " Glory to 'Mee my God, this night," in a td, a,ing manner. Messrs. G. Wallington and A. Cot- orill ako took part in the meeting.

div.head: 'UTE EXAMINER SATURDAI, JULY 7, 1894,
div.p: 'UTE EXAMINER SATURDAI, JULY 7, 1894,
ANNUAL WORKS TRIPS.

On Saturday the following well-known Warring- ton firms took advantage of the exceedingly fine weather to have their annual workmen's trip to various seaside places. One effect of this was a noticeable decrease in the number of Saturday night "shoppers." The total number of people who left Warrington by these trips being over 2,000.

div.head: AIAVVSON AND CO.'S EXCURSION.
div.p: AIAVVSON AND CO.'S EXCURSION.

The above excursion to new Brighton and back on the Ship Canal by the splendid steamer Snowdrop, took place on Saturday last, when between 300 and 400 persons availed themselves of the opportunity to make the passngo down the canal. A start was made about 8 o'clock from Latch- ford Locks in most delightful weather and great interest was taken during the passage of the many great accom- plishments of the engineers' art. Runcorn, Weston, Saltpert and Ellesmere port, with their shipping of all sizes, came in for a share of attention, Eastham Locks being reached about 11 o'clock, and after a splendid run down the Mersey, the steamer arrived at Princes landing stage about 12 o'clock, where a number of the party landed to see the sights of Liverpool, the remainder pro- ceeding to New Brighton. About 100 of the party proceeded with the steamer to her anchorage and par- took of an excellent luncheon provided by Mawson and Co., after Vk hich dancing was indulged in on the saloon deck for a short time. After a stroll on the sands the time for the return journey arrived. The party embarked on the steamer and a start was made for home about 5.40 p.m., and between this point and the Liverpool landing stage the trippers were treated with a sight of the concluding stage of the race between the splendid yachts Britannia and Satanita. Here the remainder of the party were taken up and proceeding onwards, Latchford was reached about 9.15 p.m. thus concluding a most excellent excursion by water which everyone thoroughly enjoyed. Mr. R. Scarisbrick and party contributed the musical portion of the programme to the intense satisfaction of everyone. The catering which was undertaken by Mr. E. Lake was carried out in a most efficient manner. RICHMOND AND CO.

About 700 of Messrs. Richmond and Co.'s employes and friends left Bank Quay station at 6.50 a.m.for Blackpool which was reached about eight o'clock. Here the excur tionists dispersed and proceeded to the different places of amusement in the town. The trip tickets, it may be mentioned, gave free admission to Raike's Hall. At 1.30 a number of foremen and friends, including Mr. and Mrs. Richmond gathered together at Barratt's Victoria Hotel for dinner. After the meal Mr. W. R. Stevenson, who is leaving the firm, received a handsome gold chain and medallion inscribed "Presented to Mr. W. R. Stevenson as a token of respect and esteem by the offi- cials and emplo, es of Messrs. Richmond and Co.,Warring- ton, June 30, 1894." The afternoon was spent in vari- ous wass. Aquatic sports were indulged in by some, much interest being manifested in the swimming races. The trippers reached home safely at about half-past ten. This is die third annual trip provided by Messrs. Richmond and Co. _ _ _

SANKEY WIRE MILLS. The employes of the Sankey Wire Mills held their annual excursion on Saturday, the place of resort being S uthport. About 400 left the Central Station at 7.35 a.m., and arrived at Southport at about nice o'clock. The day was beautifully fine although it was rather too hot for pleasure. The Winter Gardens, and the Botanical Gariens,and the various places of interest and amusement were well patronised. The marine lakes were favourite places for the amusement of those who en- joyed boating. Th,- pleasure yachts and steamers received the:r full shareof attention from the trippers. After a very pleasant day, the excursionists left Eouthport at 8.35. and arrived home safely at about 10 30. The arrange- ments were in the hands of a committee elected by the workmen, the secretary being Mr. John Foden.

div.head: W 111TECROSS WORKS.
div.p: W 111TECROSS WORKS.

A large number of the employe of the Whitecross Company, Limited, with their wives and friends, and a number of the employ& of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Company, with Christ Church choir, Latchford,and Sankey Church Bible Class, were conveyed by special train to Blackpool on Saturday. The excursionists left Bank Quay high level station at 6.40 a.m., and, after a good run, arrived in Blackpool at 8.40. The weather was charming throughout the day, and it enabled the pleasure-seekers to visit the principal places of interest in thi4 popular watering place. They left Blackpool for the return journey at 9.7., arriving safely at Warring- ton at eleven o'clock. The trip arrangements were successfully carried out by a committee, consisting of Messrs. Robert Webster, Dtvld Fanshaw,William Char- noek, Edward Hardman, James Buckley, John Massey and Samuel Dunbobbin (secretary). The number of ex- cursionists is estimated at about 800.

div.head: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCILS
div.p: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCILS
SCHOLARSHIPS.

It will be seen from our advertising columns that the Technical Education Committee of the Cheshire County Council is offering for competition a large number of very important scholarships. The dairy scholarships, tenable at the County Council Institute, Worleston. are to enable daughters of farmers and cottag,ers to obtain careful instructions, both practical and theoretical in cheese-making and butter-making. These now offered form the third set awarded during the present year. It may he interesting to draw attention to the number of per- sons now holding scholarships under the scheme of the County Council, and for which a sum of £2500 has been set apart for the year ending March 31st 1895. Class I. scholarships opened to pupils from elementary schso's and tenable at secondary schools of these 35 were granted in 1893, and 30 of these have been renewed for a second year. In addition 35 new ones were granted in April last, thus making a total of 65 under this class. Class 11. Special day scholarships :—Five of these were granted last year—two tenable at Owens College, and three at University College,Liverpocl, and are still being held. Bangor scholarships for higher education in agri- culture, tenable at Bangor University for two or three years ; six students are in residence at Bangor under this class, and two more have now been granted. Dairy spholarships : One set of eleven has been held at Worles- ton, and another set of nine is now being held there. Domestic scholarships s Four students are at the Bir- mingham and Midland school of cookery, receiving full courses in csokery, laundry work, and dressmaking. Sick Nursing: we students are now undergoing a three years training at the Royal Southern Hospital,Liver- pool. It is gratifying to add that most satisfactory re- ports are received in regard to the conduct, diligence, and attention of the scholarship holders. In every case the value of a scholarship is sueh as ti cover the fees charged at the institution,and the cost of railway travelling to ascl from the classes. In the case of the dairy scholarships, Bangor scholarships, domestic scholarships, and sick nursing it covers also cost of board and lodging at the Institution. A scholar- ship in music has recently been offered. The applicants will be examined by Dr. Bridge at the Cathedral prac- tising Room, Chester, on Tuesday next. At the meeting of the Technical Instruction Committee on Friday last week, Bangor seholarships were awarded to Alan Baeulsy, df Stockham,Runcorn, aud J.F. Black- shaw of Marton.

div.head: BLACKBURN MIRACLE.
div.p: A BLACKBURN MIRACLE.
SAFETY FOR MILL OPERATIVES.

The debt Which the world's progress owes to accidents must be large, but the exact debt we may never dis- cover. To one case only do we now wish to draw our readers' attention,but it is of the first importanca to the thousands who work in Lancashire and other mills,often under circumstances, if unalterable, certainly not of the beat. Our opportunity to thus make public what might have been otherwise known but to a few arose from a rumour accidentally overheard by a "Lancashire Even- ing Express" reporter, who in consequence called, for further information, on a lady whose name was men- tioned in connection with it—Mrs. Beardsworth, of 20, Cowell-st,, Blackburn.

Mrs. Beardsworth told him a history only too cornnion in every weaving centre ; but whiGh fortunately had not the pathetic end so many such cases have. She had been ill, and it was of her illness and remarkable re- covery that the reporter inquired. At first Mrs. Beards- worth said, it was only an ordinary cold, but it stuck to her for twelve months. She could not sleep for severe fits of coughing, during which great lumps of phlegm gathered in her throat. Such a state of affairs could not long continue without effecting her general health, and it is not surprising that she was soon unable to get about. A bed was put up for her downstairz and near .a fire; and there she remained until, by the suggestion of a sister who had read in the newspapers of the ex- traordinary recovery of patients treated by the new discovery in medical science, she was led to the use of Dr William's Pink Pills for Pale People. Mrs. Beardsworth's experience has already spread the knowledge of Dr. W illiams' Pink Pills among people in the neighbourhood. She recommends them to every weaver. Weaving in time enfeebles many a once hardy constitution. div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
PROPOSED GENERAL MANAGER.

The Ship Canal Committee of the Manchester Cor- poration considered at a recent meeting the important question, raised in a letter received by the chairman of the company from Lord Rothschild, of placing the management of the affairs of the company under one responsible head. Lord Egerton, in communicating with Lord Rothschild, said he should make it his duty to consult his colleagues, and to consider in what way the view expressed in the letter could be best carried out. The Ship Canal Board afterwards agreed to hold all special meeting on the 6th July, at which Sir Edward Jenkinson is to move the following resolutions :—(1) " That this board agrees with the opinion expressed in the letter to the chairman and the Lord Mayor, signed by Lord Rothschild, dated June 12th, 1894—namely, that a responsible head should be appointed, who will give his whole time and attontion to the management of the affairs of the company." (2) " That this head have large powers conferred upon him, and that his salary be fixed at £3,000 per annum." The Ship Canal Committee of the Corporation, having considered these proposals, resolved—" That the Lord Mayor be requested to convene a special meeting of this committee for the purpose of considering the proposed resolutions to be moved at the Manchester Ship Canal Board re the appointment of a 'responsible head.' That the committee do meet for this purpose on Friday next (29th of June) at 10 a.m., and that in the meantime a copy of the two proposed resolutions be forwarded to each member of the committee.' The committee met accordingly, and resolved unani- mously—" That the Corporation directors be advised to acquiesce in the two proposals of Sir E lward Jenkinsen set out in the minutes of this committee, vol. 3. p. 65, if the entire service of Mr. J. K. Bythell can be secured; but failing this they will he recommended not to give their approval to a general declaration unless accom- panied with a specific proposal." MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND irnE CANAL. The Manchester Corporation on Wednesday accepted the resignation of Sir John Harwood as vice-chairman of the directors on the Ship Canal Board. The recom- mendations of the Consultative Committee, including the appointment of Mr. J. K. Bythell as managing director at £3,000 a year if his services can be secured, were approved. The expediency of vesting the canal in the hands of a public trust was discussed,but without definite result.

div.head: DROWNED WHILST BITIIING AT
div.p: DROWNED WHILST BITIIING AT
R UN CORN.
TILIE INQUEST.

A sad case of drowning occurred on Friday even- ing at the Randleld Pit, Halton Lod,ge,Runcorn. A youth named William Henry Povey, aged 18 years, who had resided until his death with his parents at 63, Halton-road, went to the pit referred to with several of his companions to bathe on the occasion men- , tioned. A frer being in the water for a considerable time his friends got out and dressed themselves, leaving him swimming about. Subsequentiy he was noticed to be sinking, and he commenced to shout for assistance. No one was at hand, however, who could render the necessary help, but in a short time a young man named Frederick Rawlimson appeared upon the scene, and jumped into the water atter the youth had disappeared from the surface. After diving a second time Rawlin- son caught Povey by the ankle, and with the assistance of other persons dragged him on to the bank. Efforts were made to restore animation but with no successful result. The body was then conveyed to the home of the deceased,and his parents were apprised of the sad occur- rence. The news of the death of their son slyricked them very much. An investigation into the circumstances attending the death of the unfortunate youth was conducted by Mr. , J. E. Woisley, coroner, at Runcorn Palle° Court,on Mon- 'day morning.—Evidence of identification was given by the father of the deceased. William Povey,who said that his son left home about 7 30. Witness did not see him alive again his dead body being subsequently brought , home by the police.—Other testimony proving the above particulars was given,in addition to which it was stated that the youth was probably suffering from cramp at the time of his death.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned."—The Coroner inquired if any- thing further had been done in Runcorn since his last visit to secure public swimming baths far the town to which one of the juri men answered that the matter was being considered by a committee of the Improvement Commissioners, who had not as yet made any report. He was, however, of the opinion that in time baths would be provided in the town.. Deceased was connected with the St. John's Presby- terian Church, was a scholar in the Sunday school, and a member of the Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour. On Sunday morning and afternoon, the pastor, the Rev. J. Pafford Williams, made very feeling allusions to the death of the youth, who he said had been an earnest Christian, and had been active in prac- tical work for the good of the Church and Sunday schools.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
DRUNKENNESS.

At the Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. John White, Joseph Nlitchell, farm labourer, Pon:- ton, was charged with having been drunk on the 19th of May at Poulton. Prisoner was also charged with drunkenness on the 22nd of May and the. Ist of June. On the two first charges Mitchell was summoned to appear at the Warrington County Petty ,Sessions,and on his failing to do so a warrant was issued again,t him. P.C.Head proved the three charges. On the first two the fine of 10s. and costs NV as imposed and on the last ss. and costs, or in de- fault of payment 14 days' imprisonment. Prisoner went to gaol.

div.head: OPEN-AIR TEMPERANCE WORK.
div.p: OPEN-AIR TEMPERANCE WORK.

An open-air temperance meeting was held on the open space behind the British Workman Public- house, Bewsey-st., on Sunday night. Mr. John Drury delivered an earnest opening address. Mr. Wm. Roberts followed with a spirited appeal for workingmen to sign the temperance pledge and look well to their home duties. Mr.lf.laylor,P.C.Nl., deplored the large number of drunken women he had seen during the week. They wanted men of backbone in Warrington to associate with temper- ance men and fight the drink question. Drink des- troyed more souls than all other sources of evil known. Tnirteen brewers held a capital of over .C 13,000,000 saved over £l,OOOOOO, but only paid about £130,000 annually in wages. Mr. Adam 'for- rocks also spoke. The meeting was largely at- tended, and peaceable throughout._

RETURN OF THE MILITIA. TO WARRCNGTON. The 3rd and 4th Militia Battalions, King's Regi- ment, Liverpool, reurned to Warrington after six weeks' encampment at Altcar on Saturday. The first portion arrived by train at Bank Quay Station about half-past ten and the second portion an hour afterwards. They were marched through Sankey- St. and liorsemarket-st. to Orford Barracks, where later on in the day they were dismissed. Colonel Garraway was in command of the 3rd and Colonel Woodward the 4th battalion. The men went, throng the full course of training and musketry drill. Their behaviour during the whole of training was of a most exemplary character, and on Tuesday of last week the inspecting officer, Colonel Eyre Wil- liams, complimented them on this score, speaking in very flattering terms of their conduct and the excellence of their drill. On :11onrf.ay afternoon the 3rd Militia Battalion South Lancashire Regi- ment left Warrington by special trains for Chipping, where they will undergo twenty-seven days' train- ing in camp. The men, 800 in number, were under the command of Colonel Malley. NEW CURATES AT THE PARISH CHURCH.

The Rev. G. B. Thurston. M.A., and the -Rev. Henry Robert Mackenzie Hutt, 8.A., curates of the Parish Church, read themselves in at the service in the church on Sunday morning. Mr. Thurston is senior curate and Mr. Mackenzie Hutt has re- cently been appointed deacon._
THE TOWN- CLERK AND MRS. WHITTLE AT LONDON.

The Lord nayor of London gave a ball at the Mansion House on Friday night, for the purpose of meeting the Mayors and provosts of England and Wales. In the absence of the Mayor and Mayore,s (Alderman and Mrs. Greenall) Warrington was re- presented by the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) and Mrs. Whittle. On the following day Mr. an,. Nlrs. Whittle attended the opening of the new Tower Bridge. PRESENTATION AT BUCKLEY-STREET CHAPEL.

A few days ago Mr. J. Richardson bandmaster to the Buckley-street Sunday School Brass Band, received a handsome brass music stand in recognf- tion of Lis services. Mr. Scott made the presenta- tion, and Mr. Trow having made a few remarks, Mr. Richardson suitably responded.

div.head: FLOWER. SERVICE AT DARESBURY
div.p: FLOWER. SERVICE AT DARESBURY

A flower service was held in Ile Parish Church qt 2.45, on Sunday afternoon, when the Church Sunday school scholars from Moore, Hatton, Daresbqry,and Preston Book attended, each carrying a bunch of flowers. Special hymns were very creditably ren- dered by the choir, and an interesting address was given by the Rev. G. Wray, vicar of Halton, frou, the words, "Consider the lilies." At the conclusion ot the service the flowers were presented to the Warrington Union Workhouse,and kindly con veyed thither by Mr. Thomas Warburton. BELL-RMGERS AT GRAPPENIIALL.

On Sunday the bell-ringers ot Grnppenhall Church rang a peal of 720 bob minor (18 bobs and two singles) in 23 minutes for service the sixth being the observation bell. The following was the order in which they stood :-Ist James Mainwarin, (conductor); 2nd,Frede.rick T. Spence.; 3,d, Thoma- Burrows; 4th S. Horsfall ; .115th1 C. R. Grtenall .; J. W. Booth. Tenor, 10ewt. 2rs. The above is Mr. Greenall's first peal.

div.head: TRAP ACCIDENT.
div.p: TRAP ACCIDENT.

At a little before 10 on Monday morning Mr. Porritt, of the Willows, Orford, was driving, in his trap down Academy-street when the pmy and he was thrown to the ground. Mr. Porritt,who was severely cut about the forehead, was taken to the Infirmary, where, after having the wouu,i dressed, he was discharged. P.S. A. AT THE Y. . A.

In connection with the above a largely attanded meeting was held on Sunday. Mr. H. C. Jones pre- sided. The Rev. W. J. Kirkland de!ivered an able address on "The importance ()revery man perform - in his duty in the sphere in which he moved " Much interest was manifested in the homely and forcible illustratigns which were given. Mr. Taylor gave an excellent recital, and Mr. Lunt (secretary), and Mr. Kent (president) also took part, in the meeting. LOST CHILDREN ON WALKING DAY.

There was a considerable number of lo,t children in Warrington on Walking Day. There were on fewer than 20 children lost for several hour, all however, being discovered by their parents and friends before midnight. One boy, who &aid he wHs five years of age, but could give neither his ;la ae nor address, was taken to the Police-station atter eleven o'clock at night. Admirable order was kept by the police, notwithstanding the large crowds which assembled in the principal streets. I nip.ctor Bowen, who was, as usual, in charge of the :-,treet traffic, deserved special prake for his labours throughout the day. A "SMASH" AT LATCHFORD.

On Monday night at about half-pasr 11 a large hank engine which was in the siding at ',itch- ford ran off the line and plunged deeply into the bank. It seems that the engin, was shunted into the siding to make way for a passenger train. It is said that the driver, thinking that he was on the main line, put steam on and dashed at Nil speed into a stop-block which was placed at the end of the siding. The stop-block was smashel into bits and driven a distance of 15 yards, and the engine which weighs about 50 tons was thrown off the line and embedded, tender first, in the bank. Fortun- ately no one was hurt though the driver and fire- man had a providential escape, as at:tither three yards would have carried the engine over a hri ige and into the road below, a distance of about 30 foot. Very Ittle damage was done to the engine, which was got out on Tuesday. THE LATE CEMETERY REGISTRAR.

Reference was made to Mr. J. P. Leigh, the late registrar of the Cemetery, by the Hector, at the Parish Church on Sunday morning. The deceased gentleman hal been for over 50 years a member of the St. Elphins choir. For five or ten minutes the Pector spoke in a very impressive manner about the deceased, making mention of his kind disposi- tion and generosity. He was in harness almost up to the day of his death, being suddenly stricken down and rendered unconscious, in which state he remained until his death. His was a life which might serve as an example to many, as he felt, sure that he was quite prepared for death. lie (the rec- tor) had been associated with him for several years; and had frequently met him at th e cemetery,and beau greatly struck by his devotion and by his sym- paty for those who had lost relatives and friends by death.

div.head: iItISSARS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: iItISSARS AT WARRINGTON.

The fourteenth Hussars, to the number of about 100, arrived in Warrington at noon on Saturday from Manchester, and were billeted at various hotels and public-housesthrough the week-end. On Sunday morning the band of the r,giment played a selection of music in Rylands-street. The regi- ment left the town on Monday morning for Liver- pool en route to Ireland. The, departure of the men was witnessed by a large number of the punlic and the fine animals or which he men were mounted were particularly admired.

The Fashion correspondent of a London paper says : each year there is a dominant note in Fashion; this year it is sILK. Since the early ',art cf May we have looked at, talked of, a• d written about English Silks until even the most unobservant isave bad it borne. in on them that at last, if somewhat late in the day, we have discovered that we are neglecting one of our oldest British Indus- tries, and have now made up our minds to make silk, manufactured at home, really fashionable. That the recent National Silk Exhibition has already done good.it is easy to see. All our largest Silk Mercers now keep in Stock, end make up the products of English looms, and at really rf-asonable prices ; the quality of the materials being far better than the foreign cheap Silks with which this country has of late years betn flooded. It is satis- factory to know that large orders hare been placed with English Silk Weavers by the Queen, members of the Royal Family, and Ladies of high position in society. Now it is only for the multitude to follow the good example set, and /Cm lish Silk will, by degrees, regain the foremost place in the market. Taffeta glace, of which there were many cha: ming examples at the London Silk Exhibition, is admirably adapted for the all-silk gowns and blouses now so fashionable.

SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1894.

THE celebration of General Boom's A Jubilee, jubilee,' which has taken place this week, is an event which deserves more than a passing notice. It is safe to say that, apart from the Salvation Army, there is no other existing organization—religious or other- wise—which could have brought such a various crowd together as gathered at the Crystal Palace on Wednesday to do honour to its chief. The Salvation Army is cosmopolitan in the fullest sense of the word, and this fact must have been forcibly impressed upon the minds of Londoners during the present week. We are told that the mnititude which filled "the great glass house" included men and women of all nations, black, white, and yellow, who jostled each other pro- bably for the first and last trine, and their cos- tumes were even more varied than their features. The headquarter staff of the " Army " are adepts at organising spectacular displays, and it was cer- tain that, considering the wealth of material they had at command, they would not fail on this occasion. As usual, the military models upon which most of the operations of the Salvation Army are framed, were adhered to. There was a "march past" and a "jubilee review." General BOOTH drove up amidst the enthusiastic acclamations of his forces, and he witnessed four- teen battalions and sundry cavalry brigades defile past at "saluting point." . •

Although General BOOTH has given fifty years of, strenuous labour in the field of religion this jubilee' does not bring with it any -abatement of zeal or energy. It need not, however, be said that the Salvation Army has not been in existence tho. whole of these fifty years. General BOOTH dates his jubilee from 1844, when he was fifteen years of age. He was at that time amongst the Wesleyans, but a few years later he became a minister of the Methodist New. Connexio*. In the end his ardour for evangelical work impelled him to strike out a path of his own, and after carrying on for some yeais a "Christian Mission in the East of London, he finally launched the Salvation Army in 1878. The methods of the Array; though they have beenunsparingly condemned and reprobated by .many people, were amazingly successful: Branches were established in all parts of the country, and one foreign country after another was " invaded "1 by the "Hallelujah Lasses." The experiences of ; these intrepid evangelists was of a varied character, and in not a few instances they had to suffer persecution of a serious character. We ' are now told by General BOOTH himself that there are four thousand officers abroad and that the : Army is installed in thirty-seven different countries and colonies. What the future has in store for Salvationism it is, of course, impossible to predict. General BOOTH is himself as full of faith in his wonderful organisation as ever lie Was. It was, he says, intended for the benfit of mankind throughout the world, and it only needs courage and faith to accomplish their ideal. Salvationists are, undoubtedly, abundantly supplied with both faith and courage, but, as to whether these qualities will save the Army from that rapid decay which some people like to predict, must: be left to the coming years to decide.

LAST week the Warrington The Vaccination Board of Guardians rescinded by Officership. a majority of fourteen to two the resolution dismissing Dr. GORNALL from the post of vaccination officer. On the whole there is, per- haps, no cause for surprise at this complete rever- sal of the decision arrived at a month ago. There was really nothing to be said for the resolution. It was unexpectedly sprung upon a small meeting of • the Board and even then it was carried by a majo- rity of one only.. The ruling of the Clerk and the protests of the minority were ignored, though it is quite clear that no public body could conduct its business in this style without bringing itself into confusion and contempt. *After the resolution was passed some of its promoters and supporters seem to have quickly become ashamed of their own -smartness. It was soon found that the peremptory dismissal of an officer who had given over twenty years of service without any cases of complaint did not commend itself to anybody's sense of fair- ness. The only reason that had been adduced for the action taken was seen to be an extremely flimsy one, and . w'o.atever force it might have had in the estimation of some people has been demolished by the memorial which has been signed by, we believe, all but two of the medical men of • the town. It is not stir- prising to learn from the debate on Wednesday that some of the most influential men of the Con- servative party in the town, including the mem- laer for Parliament, Mr. R. PIERPOINT, have been anxious to bring about the rescinding' of the resolution. The Conservative party is, on the whole, responsible for the class of men who repre- sent Warrington on the Board of Guardians, and it was getting q uite clear that the actions of some of them needed, in the interest of the Party, just a little supervising. They seemed to be on the high road for introducing into Warrington methods of dealing with public officials which are blamed for a vast amount of local corruption and misgovernment in America. For whatever might be given as the ostensible reason for Dr. GO.R- NALL's dismissal the popular impression was, even amongst Conservatives themselves, that he was being struck at because of his opinions on certain public questions. Had the resolution been adhered to this impression would have re- mained in spite of all disclaimers. .
