MINERAL WATER. MANUFACTURERS AND THEIR BOTTLES. At the Widnes Police Court on Thursday, Margaret Hynan, of 3, Hutphinson-street, Widnes,was summoned on two informations at the instance of F. Bastow, the inspector of the Liverpool and District Mineral Water Manufacturers' Association, for applying a false trade description to certain beer of her own manufacture which she had put into bottles belonging to Robert Ryder, of St. Helens, a member of the association. The prosecution was brought under the Merchandise Marks Act -of 1887. The objects of the association having been explained by Mr. Berry, and ewes in support of the prosecution cited, the bench pointed out to the de- fendant that she had rendered herself liable to a penal,ty of £2O or an Alternative of four months imprisonment; but as the solicitor of the association did not wish for a heavy sentence, they inflicted a fine of is. and costs (125.) on each information, or fourteen days imprison- ment. The bench also warned the defendant against a repetition of the offence. COLLIER'S is. BUTTER is the gem in the market.— Advt. TESTING THE RUNCORN DOCKS FIRE B WOAD&

With a view of testing the capacity and promptness of the men of this brigade in answering a call, a false alarm was made on Friday evening. Some old timber on the South Pier had bees set on fire purposely and the" box. ze'r" ,was sounded at 7.30, when all the men were at home. In fifteen minute a sufficient number of men had arrived and connected the hose with the hydraulic mains and steam force pump, and were playing upon the burning timber. A new buzzor had been fixed to one of the engines, but it was found to be incapable of making itself distinctly heard by some of the men, in and about the Top Locks. However, everything was done with praiseworthy despatch, and there is no doubt that if the alarm had been clearly heard by all,the time would have been shortened. When everything is considered, the result of the experiment will be found to be very satis- factory. The water supply was good, as from the hydraulic main the water could be thrown across the Ship Canal. COLLIER'S FRES)" IRISH DAIRY BUTTER, 10d. per lb is excellent—Advt. SUMMER VACATION OF ST. PAUL'S DUMB CLASS, RUNCORN.

The members of this class, by way of bringing their 1 meetings to a pleasant temporary close during the sum- mer months, held what was termed "A musical after- noon "on Sunday—in the morning chapel of St. Paul's. There was a large assembly of teachers and members. Mr. George Bellamy teok the chair in the absence of the president, Mr. B. Kniveton. In his opening address the Chairman observed that he was very pleased to see such a large attendance of members. They had enter- tained the hope that the gathering would be a success, and it was surely a pleasure to all to see that their wish had been gratified. It was tdear fronri the number pre- sent that the members highly appreciated the ability of, the gentlemen who were helping them that day with their instruments. He alluded to Mr. W. Kay's string quartette party. .Musical, selections were given in a manner worthy of praise by the above combination, which consisted of Messrs.' W. Kay, C. Ditchfield, J. Marlow, and W. Simkin. Two cornet solos were ren- dered by Mr. Robert Pierpoint, who was accompanied by the quartette party and the organ. Mr. W. Kay ' executed with skill a violin solo with organ accompani- ment. Miss Heatherington was heard to special ad- vantage in her rendition of "The Better Land, which she sang with much feeling. At the conclusion the Chairinan thanked all those ladies and gentlemen who had assisted that afternodn, and he hoped that when the class re•assembled in September they would be f Ortunate enough to secure the help of their musical friends again. The singing of the Doxology and the pronouncing of the Benediction brought a very pleasant afternoon to a close.

RUNCORN CYCLING CLUE.

The Saturday riders of this club congregated in Devon- shire Square on Saturday afternoon and promptly at 230 started on a spin to Liverpool. The original place selected was Delamere,but it was afterwards decided by the members who turned up to go to Liverpool and sail across to New Brighton for the purpose of seeing the finish of the yachting race. The run to the former city was much enjoyed and the sail across the Mersey to New Brighton was Equally as pleasant. Tea haying been par- taken of they spent a short time in various kinds of amusements, and having again sailed back to Liverpool commenced the return journey on their machines arriv- ing home in good time and all very pleased with the afternoon's outing. The Wednesday section turned out in strong force on the afternoon of the abov. day, the number being seventTen. This time the desrination was High Leieh and the journey to this place was began promptly at 2 15, from Devonshire Square. The- run was one which had been specially arranged with Wigan on Wednesday,both teams joining at a certain paint and running together. High Leigh was reached at about 3.45, the riders having taken the route via. Moore and Walton. The roads were -in capital condition, and the spin proved extremely pleasant. After the members of both clubs had taken tea they engaged in a game of cricket.and su4sequently in one of rounders. Runeorn defeated their opponents on both Occasions, the cricket score being Runcern 64, Wigan 56. Later on the cycl- ists were photographed by the sub-captain, Mr. Willie Mack, each club being taken separately. Thn homeward run was enjoyed, Runcorn being reached at 9.30. Information has been given to the authorities. • RISLEY METHODIST CHAPEL. After the evening service on Sunday at the Risley Methodis:. Chapel Mr. and Mrs. John Higham were presented with a large family Bible on the occasion of their recent marriage. Mr. W. Hughes-referred in eulogistic terms to Mrs.Higham. who, he said, had attended to her duties as a teacher at the Sunday school regularly and diligently. Mr. Joseph Taylor spoke highly of Mr. Higham as a scholar in the Sunday school, and as a member of his *class, .and also of his Christian life. Mr. H.

Ezard, president of the church, Made the presenta- tion, and Mr. Higham briefly ret timed thanks.—At the close of the presentation Mr. J. Johnson (Pad- gate) publicly admitted Mr. and Mr. T. Bold, late of Widnes, but who have taken up their residence at Risley, as members of their church. Both cere- monies were witnessed by a large congregation.-- The members of the congregation held their annual trip on. Monday, when. a visit was paid to Overton Hills. The party were conveyed by 'buses supplied by Messrs. Maginn Bros., of Warrington. Dinner and tea were provided,and a ramble on the bills was thoroughly enjoyed. UTTERING BASE COIN AT CHESTER : A. WARRINGTON MAN IN TROUBLE. • At the Chester City Police Court, on Saturday, ' Thomas Wuih, ironworker, 6, Union-street, War- rington, was charged on remand with uttering a base florM at the Bars Hotel, on the 28th Jute.— Eliza Pearson, daughter of the landlord of the Bars Hotel, said that on the night in question a man named; Clavin, who appeared to be in the company of the prisoner, called for some beer, when prisoner himself jumped up and .said " Fill four pints.': Clavin said they had not time to drink more than. four glasses as it was nearly eleven. Clavin handed the flarin produced in payment. She put the coin into the drawer, and gave the man is. Gd. change. He pushed the money along the counter in the direction of the prisoner and several other men who were atanding, but she could not say whether pri- soner picked it up. Prisoner called for another glass of beer for another man, tendered Gd. in pay- ment and received 41-(1. change. Later he called for more drink for the company and paid for it., 51d.in .copper. .At eleven o'clock prisoner called for half a gallon of beer to take away with him. She served him and charged him .61. on the can. Ile paid for this with the florin produced. She gave him gd. change and .proceeded to sound the 2s:-piece. While she was din g this he asken her if she would return the Cl. when he brought the can back. She showed the flari ti to her father, who went after prisoner. She took the first, florin out of the drawer • and sounded it, and found it to be a bad one.—Prisoner when asked whether he had any questions to put to the witnesa, admitted tendering the coin. however, did not know it was base.—Detective Gallagher proved taking prisoner into 'custody from the last witness.—Witness asked him had he any money and he pulled out 6d. and 21. That was all that was found on, him. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1894.
RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMIS- SIONERS.

On Thursday morning the monthly meeting of this Board took place in the Town Hull, Mr. S. Tay- lor, J.P., presiding. The other gentlemen present were—Messrs. W. Handley, P. Speakman,J.P.,- C.C., John Meadowcroft, F. Wiswall, J. W. Lightburn,Ll. J. Once, D. Bisbrown, T. Lee, Wm. Leach, William Hankinson Walter Collier, E. Imison, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and J. Wilding (assistant surveyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. McDougall presented his monthly report, from which it appeared that 20 deaths had been registered, . _

one of which was an inquest.case, making a death rate of 12 per 1,000 of the estimated population. Exclasiye of the inquest case the death rate was 104. The number of deaths registered during the corresponding- period of last year in the district of the Authority was 71.—The Chairman said the report was extrelnely satisfactory.

HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE. This committee recommended that public conveniences he erected at Waterloo Bridge, Doctor's Bridge, and Delph Bridge at an estimated total cost of £115; also that application be made to the• Local Government Board for their sanction to a loan of that amount for 30 years. Mr. Wiswall moved the adoption of the minutes, and after some discussion this was agreed to.• '
HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The recommendations of this committee were that the plans submitted by the Bedford Leigh Brewing (Jo. for the abatement of nuisances at the " Union Vaults "and "Fox Inn " being deemed satisfactory, the same is ap- proved. That notices be serted on the managers of the Holy Trinity Schools, on the trustees or owners of the Foresters' Hall, on the trustees of the St. Luke's School, Mason-street; and on the owners of property situated 79, to'B9 and 93 Spring Gardens, and 35 to 64 Sewell-street, t.) abate certain nuisances, and make im- provements and additions to the places mentoned. Should these notices not be complied with that legal peo- ceedin,gs he. taken. That expenses of the deputation in- spec lug the refuse destructors at Warrington amounting to £2 Bs. be paid. That Walter Morris, 78, Greenway- road, be registered as a purveyor of milk. Mr. Unison proposed the confirmation of the minutes and in doing so said that the expenditure of the deputa• tion visiting Warrington had been incurred by the coin- mittee without the consent of the Board but under the circumstances he was sure no objection would be rais:.d against their action in the matter. The committee had for a long time been considering the question as to what should be done with the night soil and they had looked over alternative sites without any very satis- factory result. At length they heard of a system which had been formulated by an inventor in Warrington, and they resolved to visit that place for the purpose of in- specting the scheme without the sanction of the Board. The committee had not yet made a report but that would most probably be done shortly. Dr.-Carter Bell nad described the system as being almost perfectly ,dertruc- tive. The money spent by the deputation inspecting the system had been well spent, and the information gained might, in the near future, prove a great advantage to the ratepayers.—Mr. Lightburn in seconding said the ques- tion of more completely ridding the'town of its refuse had troubled tne committee for a long time arid if they could get a "Destructor," it would prove a great bene- fit.—The minutes were confirmed. .

. IRRECOTERABLE WATER RATES. The only recommendation of the Water Committee was that the irrecoverable arrears of the water rate amounting to £62 8. 11d., for the quarter ended June 23rd be written off. Mr. Meadowcroft moved the acceptance or the recom- mendation saying that the arrears really meant those houses from which rates bad been collected but which were now almost all empty.—Mr. Speakman seconded, _

—Mr. Grice asked how nidch of this amount represented empty houses and howmuch was owing by persons who had left the town.—Mr. Meadowcroft answered that only in one or twO cases hrtd plople left the town with- out paying their rates. About £6O repiesented empty property.—The minutes were passed.

SCHOOLS,

LAYING OF TIM FOUNDATION STONE. Thursday Was an important day in the history of Widnes, for that was the date on W'hich the founda- tion stone of a new Public Library and Technical School was laid. The new building is estimated to cost about £lO,OOO, and is to be built opposite the Town Hall, and by the side of the St. Paul's Church, so that Victoria-square, which these building en- close, will be a fine site when the school is erected.. The site of the school has been given by Captain Henry Gerard Leigh, J.P., and the Committee therefore thought it fitting that that gentleman should be asked to perform the cerem.onv of laying the foundation stone on Thursday. Captain Leigh consented, but owing to the severe illness of his child, on Wednesday he regret- fully had to send a letterstating. his inability to attend. It may be stated that his child died on Thursday morn- ing' and great sympathy was pelt for Captain Leigh on hisbereavement. The Mayor of Widnes (Alderman F. H. Gossage) had also promised to preside over the pro- ceedings, but the doctor declined to allow him to take any part in public business, and he therefore was absent from the day's proceedings. The Committee therefore had to look for two other gentlemen to undertake the work of Captain Leigh and the Mayor, and an excellent ehoice was made when they obtained the consent of Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., to lay the foundation stone, and of Councillor W. W. Gossage to preside. The square was gaily adorned Fith bunting,and a flag was also hoisted above the Town Hall on Thursday as the time for performing the ceremony drew sear, and at ahaut 1.30 in the afternoon, a procession of the Cor- ' porotion, the School Board, and other gentlemen marched from the Town Hall to the site of the new

Upon arriving at the place, Cannelllot W.W. Gossege addrOssing the large assembly,which had gathered round, said that he had first of all to apoloasso for the absence of his eather, the Miyer. He was suffering from illness at the present time, and the doctor had ordered him complete rest. His father had told him to sa'y how grieved he was at being unable to be present. Captain Leieh was also unable to be present owing to bereave- ment. He was fuse that they all felt very much for in his sorow. (Mfr. hear.) Fortunately they had a very good substitute in Mr. Timmis—(applause)—who had kindly consented to stand for Captain Leigh. M.H. Wade Deacon, J.P., C.C. (chairman of the Widnes School Board) said that it was with great pleasure that the Technical Instrution Committee had asked Mr. Timmis to lay the foundation stone. By ask- ing him formally to perform the ceremony,he would say a few words about the necessity which had arisen for the erection of schools by the Town Clerk. Twenty years ago, for the first time science and art classes had been fsrmed in Widnes, and a committee was formed, and subscriptions obtained from the local manufacturers. The work continued, and grew very quickly and Wereheld first at the Drill Hall and afterwards to the present building in Major Cross-street. They had been able to have. n chemical laboretory owing to the generosity of Mr. Gossage, the. The work went on increasing,and passed beyond the bound of a local cammittee, and it. was therefore undertaken as a public work by the late Local Board from whom it passed to the present Corporation,. In 1890 or 1891,a sum of money came unexpectedly into the hands 'of the Lancashire County Council, and he WAS glad that they devoted it to technical education, but of that sum Widnes I' received £4BO a year. This sum .had been of the greatest benefit to the town, as they were able to form I fresh classes and increase the number of their students. They,therefore,now required fresh accommodation. He heped that when the present building was complete the Widnes people would not be content simply with even- ing classes. There would be ample accommodation to teach chemistry. There was a tremendous number of people who want to the free library, as there was an average of 500 daily. It had, therefore, been found necessary to open a temporary place for boys, and this had relieved the pressure a little. It Was, however, necessary to have a fresh place, and in his opinion it was the public duty of the Corporation to supply a building which would meet the demands of this kind. He was very-sorry that the Mayor and Captain Laigh were unable to be present, but it was very satisfactory to have a man among them who could undertake the duties,and it was with reat pleasure that he asked Mr. Timmis to perform the ceremony. (Applause.) Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., then formally laid the stone, and in a bottle were pined the coins of the realm and a number of documents. After performing the ceremony Mr. Timmis addressed the gatherinf.T. He expressed hi 4 rearrl, at the absence of Captain issigh, and also mentioned his tnuoilice.nce to Widaes. He himself felt highly honoured at neing asked to perform the duty in Captain Leigh's absenc9. Refer- ring to Widne3, he said that the town had a complete educational system. They had elementary schools second to none in the country, and also a first rate grin-It-oar school. They would soon have a technical schsol which he hoped would be as successful. He wished success to the schools, and to the directors who would Garry out the arrangements.

Councillor W. W. Gossage proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Timmis for performing the duties of the after- noon. Mr. Timmis had always taken great interyst in education in Widnes. His generosity and munificPnce towards education had been equalled by few and ex- ceeded by none. The motion was carried with cheers and Mr. Timmis suitably replied. Mr. F. Neil proposed a vote of thanks to Councillor Go4sage. which was heartily received, and after Coon- cillor Gossage had replied, Gossages band, which had been in attendance during the afternoon, struck up " God save the Queen," and the party then returned to the Town Hall. They afterwards adjourned to St. Pauls Parochial rooms, where luncheon was served. Councillor W. W. C,os,sag,e presided at the luncheon, and there were also present Mr. T. div.head: FINANCE COBIXITTIE.
div.p: FINANCE COBIXITTIE.

This committee recommended that application be made to the Local Government Board for tieir sanction to a loan of £1,250 tor 60 years for the building of the Technical Ins(itute. That the offer of the Blackburn Corporation to lend £2,000 for five years, £656 for seven years, and £369 for nine years at 31 per cent. interest be accepted. Mr. Lightburn proposed the 'adoption of the reports, and the minutes. He explained that the sum £1,250 required for the Technical Institute would not be a per- manent loan although they would have to apply to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow it as such. BLit de facto the loan was only of a temporary , character. He went on to give details of the money which the Committee had already received and which has been previously set forth in these columns, and added that the donations hp to date amounted to £960. This sum included a promise of £lOO, of which there was not the slightest doubt of their receiving. The total was theref,Te brought up to £2,800 which left a balance of £1;200 to be yet procured. They might api.ily for sanction to borrow £1,250 but they were not compelled to draw the whole amount, or indeed any of it. Then , they would get £5OO from Mr. Brunner if they could raise £5OO locally. (A Commissioner: We've very , nearly got that already.) Mr. Lightburn,. continuing, said it was true they had nearly secured £5OO locally and they hoped to make the donations reach that fi.4ure shortly and then they could apply to Mr. Brunner for his original promise of £5OO. There were many circum- stances, as they would recognise, that made it difficult to meet the monthly requirements of the contractors, and lie could only appeal 'to the members of the Com- mitee and to people outside who were in sympathy with the movement to subscribe as liberally as it was possible for them to do.—The Chairman announced that Mr. Marshall had that morning received a letter from Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, .and , Co., the well-known brewers, of Warrington; stating that they had much pleasure in subscribing £5O towards the building fund 'of the Institute. (Hear, hear.) Since their last meeting a cheque for £5O had also been received from Sir John Rigby in aid of the same object. (Elear, hear.)—The minutes were passed.

LOCAL OVERSEERS IN THE RUNCORN
COUNTY COURT.

On Tuesday afternoon at the Runcorn County Court, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, John Challinor, assistant overseer of Frodsham Lordship brought an action against Samuel Harvey and Edwin Alderman, overseers of Kingsley, for the recovery of £5, due to him for services rendered from August 12th until,September 27th, 1893. Mr. Linaker, solicitor, represented the claimant, whilst the defendants conducted their own case.

Mr. Linaker said that the reason why the plaintiff did this work was that in August of last year the assistant overseer for Kingsley died suddenly, leaving his books in a very complicated state. The, overseers, Messrr. Har- vey and Alderman, on looking over them found this to be so and aske,d the plaintiff if he would put them right for them in order that they might be submitted to an auditor. In addition to examining the books, his client had gone round to the ratepayers collecting rates on five distinct occasions twice being in the company of Mr. Harvey. He had also drawn up a notice convening a ratepayers meeting and various other documents. For the whole of the work he claimed but when the account was sent to the defendants they returned it accompanied by a refusal to pay it Mr. Challiuor; the claimant supported the statement of his soliCitor saying that when Harvey asked him to put the books right he gave him (witness) to understand that he would pay him. Being questioned by Harvey he said he had not told anybody that he was doing this work on behalf of the widow of the deveased overseer ad expected nothing for it. Eli did nut say that neither the overseer nor hintself could get. anything from the Guardians for doing the work without the consent of the ratepayers. He admitted having told the defendants that their best course was to ask the Guardians to appoint someone temporerily in the place of the late assistant overseer in order that the remaining rates might be collected. lie further aelrnitted having been a candidate for the assistant overseership, but' when col- lecting rates before the election he did not solicit support on the plea that he was then assisting the widow of the deceased overseer. Neither did he advise Harvey not to pay Messrs. Linaker for auditieg the books. • Thomas Walmsley Nicholls, brother-in-law to, and bondsman for the deceased overseer, and engaged as butcher at Frodsham, said that he heard Harvey say to Challinor, "You had better take the hooks, and I will see you right." He also heard Harvey ask Cballior if the Guardians would allow the money, to which answer Wai made that if they did not the ratepayers could.— Questioned by Harvey witness denied having said that Challiner was going to look through the books for him (witness). Thomas Bell, butcher, of Runcorn, and brother-in- law of the late assistant overseer, deposed to hearing Harvey tell Challinor to look through the books, and he (Harvey) would see Challinor all right. Witness 'did not hear Challinor ask to take the books of his own accord. • Samuel Harvey denied that he had ever premised to compensate Challinor in the least for doing the wark he did. It was Nicholls that asked to take the books away and who said Challinor would look through them and put them in order. The books were taken away and Challinor examined them. The latter, accompanied him an two accasions, to collect rates, bnt he did so sorely because he was a candidate for the office of assistant averseer and wsshed to solicit support. He stated that he did not expect anything for doing what he was be- cause it was on behalf of the widor. After being re- jected at the election of assistant overseer he never came agrin. Continuine,Mr. Harvey said that if the deceased assistant overseer had lived the amount that would have been paid him for the work which Challinor, did, was 155., whereas Challinor now charged £5. John Lewis; farmer,of Kingsley, and John Littlemore, labourer, of Kingsley, both stated that Challinor had said that he did not expect anything for doing the work ef. the deceased overseer, but that what he was doing was for the benefit of the widow. He also said he was applying for the assistant overseership and asked wit- nesses for their votes.
Edwin Alderman, the other defendant, re-echoed the words of the previous witnases. He had never beard Flarvey promise Challinor anything for doing the wprk ,neither did he himself.

His Honour, in smut-I)in.. up, saki that he could not think in the fAee of th evidence that the defendants had made themselves personally responsible for what Challi- nor did. He was of .the opinion that Challinor did the work for the purpose of securing votes and took his chance of getting payment for his services from the ratepayers. He could do nothing more but enter judg- ment for defenthuts.

div.p: RAITON.

LOCAL SUCCOSS.—We are pleased to notice that Mr. Alan ltagule?,• son of Mr. Joseph Baguley, of Stockham, has succeeded in obtaining a scholarship in agriculture. _valued £4O, which was offered with another by the Cheshire County Council. The examinations were held in June at Crewe, and the pleasing result has but recently been made known. The scholarship is tenable for two years at Bangor University. Mr. Jeacock, head master of the Halton Grammer, School,'prepared Mr. Alan Baluley for the last examination. The COUNTY Rare Basis.—Mr. Thomas Davies pre- sided over a rodent meeting of ratepayers at the over- seer's office, convened for the purpose of considering the basis for county rates, as proposed by the Chealeire County Council. The subject was somewhat exhaus- tively-discussed, after which it was proposed by Mr. T. Riley, and seconded by Mr. T. rlam—" That, assum- ing that the proposed basis throughout .the county is upheld, this meeting has no objection to such proposed basis of the Ownship of Frodsham." .4211,760 is the pre- sent basis for Frodsha.m, whilst the proposed new basis is £14,052. The net poor rate assessment for December, 1893, was £13,127, since which the Manchester Ship ICanal has been rated, and the present poor rate assess- ‘ment has been increased to £14,219.

FUNERAL OF A. LATE RUNCORN RESIDENT. The remains of the late Mr. Wm. Elazlehurst. aged 47, of Robert-street, Halton,road, Ruticorn, who died some- what suddenly on Satnrday Morning, were interred in the cemetery at Overton on Tuesday afternoon. The Runcorn Town and District Band, of which the deceased had been a member no to the time of his death, accom- panied the body from Holton-road to the Railway Stotion, add thenee by train to Fiodsham. They re-formed at the Station and proceeded towards the burial place at a slow and mournful pace. The band played the Dead March in Saul both on their way.to Runcorn Station and on their way to Overton Cemetery. The coffin was of polished oak, on the top of which were several floral tributes and also the instrument and hat of the deceased. The body was bbrne by six of the deceased's friends, namely, Messr3. James Corker, Thomas Dutton, John Ford; Sainutl Stubbs, Wm. Gibbons, and Wm. Faulkner. The coffin was provided by the deceased man's fellow workmen at the Sprinch Works.

div.head: NEWTON RACES.
div.p: NEWTON RACES.

In consequence of the race meeting at Newton taking place this week, the various works in the district will be closed. All the engineering works will close on Thursday evening until Monday morn- ing, and the Sankey Sugar Works will close on Fri- day at noon. There is no doubt. there will be a large exodus of the townspeople on Friday to various places,but this is certain to be greatly counteracted by the influx of patrons of the national sport.

RACE SUNDAY. Sunday last being the Sunday preceding Newton Races, has for a great many years been termed Race t=unday. The gaieties which for a long time existed about Newton Common on that thy have now entirely died away, and there was' nothing' to in- dicate that the day was anything but an ordinary Sunday. In the evening a good number of people could be seen in the vicinity of the race course, at- tracted there no doubt out of curiosity. FLOWED. SERVrCE AT Sr. JOHN'S CHuRcH. On Sunday special flower services were held in St. John's Church, Earlestown. The transept of the church was nicely decorated with flowers, and the school children during the service made floral . offerings to the officiating minister. The pulpit at the morning and afternoon services was occupied by the Rev. W. A. Jones, curate of Golborne, and in the evening by the Rev. E. W. W. Kaye. The choir at the afternoon and evening service sang the an- them " What shall I render unto the Lord ?'' The collections, which were in aid of the Sunday school treat, amounted during the 'day to over :£5.
EIRLESTOWN WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

• The first annual picnic in connection with this association took- place on Saturday afternoon in beautiful weather. The party numbering about 100 left Earlestown about 1.30 for Lea Green, and on arrival there they proceeded to Micklehead Green, where a field and the schoolroom were kindly placed at their. disposal by Messrs. Rawlins and Sens of Rainhill, Mrs. Rawlins being the president of the as,ociation. Various games were -indulged in until tea time, when -tea was served in the schoolroom. The ladies afterwards enjoyel them- selves in various ways, .several of the paying a visit to the blue works of Messrs. Rawlins. ,00 the 7,4 urn journov after nine o cloa.

div.head: ST HELENS TOWN" COUNCIL.
div.p: ST HELENS TOWN" COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the St. Helens Town Council was held on 'Wednesday, under the chair- manship of the Deputy Mayor (Councillor F. R. Dixon-Nuttall), and the business was disposed of la twenty-fire minutes. Alderman Gamble, C.8.,-chairman of the Watch Com- mittee, moved the confirmation of the minutes, and called attention to the fact that the Local Government Board had sanctioned the appointment of Dr. John Robertson as public analyst of the borough.—Mr. Mearns suggested that when the committee again advertised for tenders for clothing for the.police force they might con- sider the desirability of a lighter material for the very hot weather.—Alderman Gam b1e.C.8., replied that if he was chairman when the clothing was again considered. he would call the attention of the committee to the matter, and if he was not chairman he trusted the Town- clerk would call attention to it. fie did not know whether if was usual for borough to have separate police clothing for the hot weather, but it could be in- quired into.

- Councillor .T. B. Leach drew attention to the unpunc- tual and ineffectual train service between St. Helens and Liverpool and St.Helens and Manchester. He said that during the coal strike trains were taken off, and they had not been renewtd. The existing service frUzn the North was so often late at St. Helens that business men frequently missed important appointments in Liverpool. He thought there should be two or three trains a day starting from St. Helens, and running direct to Liver- pool.—Alderman Gamble thought if the London and North-Western Railway gave more facilities to St.Hclens it would bo good for both. They might complain that traffic had diminished very much, but if a tradesman wanted custom he did not keep his shop stfort Of goods; and if the railway company kept St. Helens .short of trains, they would not find it good for either the com- pany mr the town. . .

- Since the passing of the St. Helens Corrmation ACt, 1893, by which the four townships of the borough were made into ene vestry, the Corporation have been face to face with the question of compensation to be paid to assistant overseers removed from offic.,e under the Act.— The Council decided to grant Mr. John Kitchen,formerlv assistant overseer for the townships of Parr and Sutton, an annuity of £84.; payable quar:erly, during the re- mainder of his natural life.

div.p: WaNCORN COUNTY COT:RT.

TUESDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes CLAIMS FOR DRAPERY SUPPLIED.—An action to recover the sum of £1 15s. 3d. was brought tee- Mr. James Herd, draper, of Manchester, against Thomas Sweetman, 27, Cartwright-street, Runcorn.—Mr. Burton, solicitor, appeared for the claimant, who stated that the wifeof the defendant had dealt with him from 1885 until her ' death. The defendant had not personally paid him any- thing but he had accompanied his wife when she came to pay instalments. Tao amount claimed was the bal- ance of the account, and was for flannel, sheets, Defendant denied denied having ever been present with his wife when she paid anything- to the plaintiff. He had never authorised his wife to procure the things on credit and he was not aware that she had done as. When plaintiff visited defendant's house for the money in November the latter said he had asked the plaintiff to send him a ha of the articles ashe knew nothing about the matter. If the hill was sent he (defendant) proinised to make inquiries and see what he could do. The bill had never been sent. ln the meantime he had examined his drawer but could • find no papers relating to any debt owing to plaintiff. ,Defendant, continuing, said be gave his wife during her life 245. per week and bought thd children's clothes, so that she always had plenty of money for her immediate , needs. Judgment was entered for defenciant.—James , Curzon, o: Lestock, was also sued by Mr. Thomas Herd, draper, Manchester, for £3 103. 6d., value of drapery which plaintiff had supplied to the wife of the defend- ant. Mr. Burton represented the claimant,who said the account was opened in 1887,and the slim mentioned was the balance of that account. Defend-sat denied liability as he had never given his wife any authority to get things on credit in this way. None of the articles de- tailed by the plaintiff had been bi,ught into the house of the defendant according to his keowledge. His wife had run away from him, but previous to her flight he had several times asked her if she owed anything. Her only answer had been, "You must find out." He allowed kis wife £2 per week when she lived with him. His Honour gave judgment for the defendant, saline that no evidence had been produced to show that the defend- ant had authorised his wite to procure the articles claimed for. I UNSUS MINED ACTION FOR WAGES DUE. Francies Edward Marks of Runcorn, sued Edward : Worthington, contractor, of Droylsden, near Manchester,' for the sum of £2 6s. Bd., balance of account for work done by plaintiff for defendant in May last.—Mr. Arthur Linaker, solicitor, Runcorn, represented the plaintiff, and the defendant was represented by Mr. V. A. Lake, solicitor, of Runcorn.—According t 6 the case of the claimant he was engaged by the defendant to remove certain timber, which the latter said was lying at Fred- sham Marsh ,into a canal boat owned by Messrs. Simpson anc Davies, Runcorn. An agreement was come to by both parties that plaintiff should pay 5 1. per hour to as many men as he thought necessary, and should himself receive 6s. per day for superintending them. Plaintiff accordingly engaged six men to do the -work, but on making enquiries he found that the timber was not lying , at Frodsnam Marsh as stated, but at Ince, several miles laway. In.consequence of the timber being such a dis- tance from Runcorn the men employed by the plaintiff would not walk thither, and consequently rode by train. Certain sums had been paid by detendant to plaintiff on account but the balance 01 £2 6s. Bd. was still due.— The plaintiff was called and 'supported his solicitor's statement. He added that after finding out the real' circumstances he wrote to the defendanteexplaining the matter to him and asked him to come over on Friday afternoon, 25th May, which was the day after the work had been commenced. He stated in the letter that the barge was nearly full, and he wished the defendant to come there in order that he might arrange to pay the - men. He had received no cheque from the defendant according to the latter's promise. Defendant did not Come over until Saturday morning, when he paid plain- tiff £2 10s. on account. He (defendant) made no corn- - plaints then about the work not beingfcompleted, and arranged to see plaintiff on Monday, and alsothe beat. , On this day claimant only took two men with him as the work was almost finished. .Whilst engaged in the work the defendant came at abent one o'clock accompanied by fire men and told plaintiff, in an excited manner,that he had taken the work out of his hands, and bad written him to that effect. Plaintiff replied that he had not re-, any such csmmunication ond asked defendant for a settlement to which the latter answered that he would pay him in a lump RUM. When plaintiff arrived home on Monday night he found a letter from the defen- dant awaiting him with the notifipation that the work had been taken out of his hands. It was dated May 26th, but the enuelope bore the date of the 28th May, show- ing that it had been despatched from Manchester on that day and had been received in Runcorn in the evening. • By Mr. Lake : It was clearly understood by the de- fendant that railway fares were to be charged, as there was no accommodation at Inca for the men. His Honour: . What! Not at Lice? Don't tell me that. •By Mr. Lake 'lt was net usual for men to pay their own lodgings when engaged in work which lasted for. such a short period. The defendant did not tell him that the timber was near Bromley's Ferry, at Lace. Mr. Lake, in his defence submitted that his client had over paid the plaintiff, and was not liable for railway fares and other small items. With regard to the num- ber of hours worked by the men his client was only liable for those which' the men actually spent in work- ing and not for the time it took them to go from their homes to the work and back again. Then, as the claim- ant did not begin working until late on Monday and finished ad early he should only be paid for half a day, 3s. The defendant had really paid . Clain:taut for more work than was done. Mr. Samuel-Worthington, the defendant, said when he made the agreement with the plaintiff he told him that the boats would have to be loaded in two days ot he would be charged for demurrage by Messrs. Simpson and Davies. No mention was made of railway fares or travelling expenses or the plaintiff would never have been engaged. his Honour gave judgment for defendant with costs.

A ST. HELENS BANKRUPTCY CAM

At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, before Mr. Begistrar Beliringer, Ambrose Fisher, a painter and plumber at- Sutton, near St. Helens, appeared on the. public examination, reprrsented by Mr. Lomax. The statement of Affairs showed liabilities £133 12s. 11d. and end assets £3O, of which £l5 had hen deposited with his solicitor for tiling the petition.—The debtor,in answer to the official receiver, st#ted that he commenced busi- ness at Sutton about elglit years ago wit'bout capital. All he had put into the business wds his savings from time to time. He had lately lost money by taking in work on new houses at low nrices,owing to competition. He had hoped te make a little prontl but had incurred a loss. Be had not kept any cash book or accounts, but the , money had gone in paying wages and accounts, and he had nothing to put away. div.head: BEFORE: THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE: THE MAGISTRATES.
IS HE AN ANARCHIST?

At the Borough Police Court on Saturday. Albert Thoyne was charged with being drunk and using foul language to a gentleman' in Manchestenlane.—P.C. Clough said he arrested the prisoner who was saying that he had come to Warrington to expose the Queen and Royal Family, that he would have his knife into them before long. He was sent to gaol for 14 days in order that he might see the folly of expressing such anarchistic principles in the public street. THE CABMEN AND THE W ATCH COMMITTEE.

A cabman named Walter Bate, was summoned at the Warrington Borough Court on Monday with being drunk in charge of a horse and waggonette on Saturday night. The defendant was observed by Constables Cooper (20), and Williamson, lying backwards upon the waggonette in Bridge-street, and also allowing the reins to be loose. They discovered that he was drunk and totally unfit to be in charge of the conveyance.—Alderman Harrison suggested that the case be reported to the Watch Com- mittee, and Inspector Bowen said that the cabmen of Warrington did not appear to have any fear of the Watch Committee at all. The defendant was fined ss. and costs.

div.head: EJECTING A BAILIFF.
div.p: EJECTING A BAILIFF.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Thursday morning, Eliza Cullen and John Cullen, mother and son, of 14, Blue Coat-st., were charged with assaulting and ejecting a bailiff named George Heacock, on the 23rd inst. The complainant stated that on the date named he went to defendant's house to take possession. As soon as he got in the 11011 Fe he was met hy the male defendant who tried to push him out. Too two defend- ants 'knocked him to the floor, broke his snectacles, and dragged him into the street. Witness's assistant was also put out by settle women. Mr. Bolton, assistant to the last witness, gave corroborative evidence. The defendants contended that tile bailiff did not enter the house but only stood on the doorstep. Mrs. Weaver, a neighbour, said the complainant knocked Mrs. Cullen to the wall in trying to get in. The magistrates imposed a fine of 103. and costs.

div.head: WIFE ASSAULT.
div.p: WIFE ASSAULT.

Patrick Hearty was charged at the Borough Court on S it- urdaywith assrlting his wife Ellen Hoarty on the Thurs- day previous. Mrs. Hoary said that on the day named the prisoner knocked ter down and kicked her while she was on the floor. When she was knocked down her head struck against the curbstone, which inflicted a very nasty wound. After the assault she went to the police station in company with a neighbour to seek protection from the prisoner.—The Chief Constable and P.C. Baxendale both deposed to seeing lier at the police station with her clothes saturated with blood from the wound in her head.—P.C. Roper said lie arrested the prisoner who was very violent and brought him t r the police station.—Mrs. Marty said she led the life of a dog with the prisoner, and hoped that the magistrates would grant an order for separation. The prisoner on being questioned denied the assault, and also said that he hoped that the magistrates would separate him from his wife, who, he said, was qnite as bad as she repre- sented him to be. He was fined 103. including costs for the assault and an order for separation was granted ; the prisoner beiapg erdered to pay 10s. per week for his wife's maintenance.
"A PRACTICAL JOKE."

Benjamin Floughton, 29, Leicester-street, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court on iNionday, with stealing four tomatoes from the cart of George Connolly, in Priestly-street, on Saturday night. The complainant did not appear, but P.c. For.ter stated that a number of young men, among whom was the defendant, were playing tricks upon Cnnnolly who had a handcart full of tomatoes. They kept knocking him about and running off with the -tomatoes. The officer drove them away several times but they persisted in their conduct,and he at length arrested the defendant and fotmd four tc,ma- toes in his possession. When the officer first noticed the cart, there were 15 or 16 boxes upon it, but when he arrested tha defendant there were only four or five left. On the following morning, he went to thc, scene of the occurrence, and found a large quantity of tomatoes strewn about the ground utterly spoiled.—The Mayor, who presided over the bench sa id that he presumed the defendant and his companions were playing a practical joke upon the complainant, but this fort of thing would have to be stopped. The defendant would be fined ss. and costs or sere.n days' imprisonment in default.

At the Warrington County Petty Sz.ssions on Wednes- day, Michabl Callighan and Thomas Houghton, of Earlestown, were charged with being drunk and dis- orderly on the Ist July at Earlestown, arid fur' her charged with assaulting the police at the same time and place. Prisoners plead& guilty to the first charge. P.C. Green deposed that on the previous Sunday nithit, Callighan was fighting another man. Witness and P.C. *Twaddle went towards him, but he ran away. They followed and took him into custody. Houghton came up and struck witness in the mouth, and the other prisoner Callighan, struck him in the face. P.C. Twaddle also gave evidenee as to being struck by both defendants in the face. Be was also struck and kicked by several persons in the crowd which assembled. In- spector Kelly said he saw the two officers in charge of the prisoner, Callighan. P.C. Twaddle was bleeding from the nose and his face was covered with blood. P.C. Green w3s also bleedid;.; from the month. Witness after- ward.; apprehended Houghten in Houghton-street. The prisoners were each fined 54. and costs or 14 days' im- prisonment for being drunk and disorderly, and 20s. and costs or one month's imprisonment for the assault upon the police.

AN 'UNHAPPY MARRIAGE.—SamueI Dunn, an iron- worker residing at Welltield-st., was summoned at the instance ef Naomi Dunn, Collin-st., for assaulting her. Mr. Browne, represented the complainant, and Mr. P. Davies, the defendant. A settlement was come to in court whereby the defendant agreed to pay the com- plainant Bs. per week. From a statement made by Mr. Davies it appeared that the defendant and complainant had only been married seven weeks, but they were unable to agree. A RACING MAN IN TROUBLE.—Robert Ball, 12 Grove Square, Liverpool, was charged with haying on the Ist June travelled on the Cheshire Lines Railway with intent to avoid payment thereof, by using a ticket which was not in use that day. Mr. P. Davies who prosecuted on behalf of the railway company, stated that the defend- ant travelled from Liverpool on the Cheshire Lines Rail- way on Thursday the 31st May to Doncaster for the races there. He took a cheap excursion ticket which was only available on the thy of issue. The defendant, however, returned on the following day, and when tickets were collected at Warringtcn station by the col- lector the defendant produced the day excursion ticket. The collector asked him for the ordinary sim.de fare, but the defendant said he only had 1.1-d. His name and ad- dress were taken,and he had written to the Clerk statiug. that he admitted the offence, hut was unable to appear. He (Mr.Davies)pressed the case as the railway company had great trouble with these racing men. Two others in the same train as the defendant committed the same offence but they had given wrong addresses. A fine of 24. 6d. and costs including the railway fare was imposed £1 13s. 9d. in all.

Hollingsworth deposed that about six o'clock the prev- ious evening he met the prisoner in Marsh House-lane, and as he appeared to have a military bearing about him, witness put some questions to him. His answers not being satisfactory witness brought prisoner to the police station. He denied being a deserter. Witness Looked through the Gazette and found that he had deserted from his regiment since 1892. The prisoner gave several false names and different regiments. The magistrates remanded him to Strange- ways to await an escort. P.C. Hollingsworth applied for the usual reward. BLll,arel Josenh Nield were charged with Sunday gambling an the 24th inst. in Nelson-st., Runcorn.— Bowles, Knowles, Robinsnn. Fish, • Brookes and Ball denied the offence.—Sergeant Lee said that at about 11.30 on the previous Sunday morning he watched the defendants fnr twenty minutes playing at "pitch and toss" in Nelson-st. Fie concealed himself behind a wall and through a small hole saw the whole of the -defend- ants engaged in the game. Money was passed between them,and just as he was jumping over, some cnins`were thrown into the air, and a few fell upon his own head, —P.C.'s Gregory and Richardson gave corrohlrative evidence after which Superintendent Atherton remarked that Monday after Monday convictions were made in that court against youths for this Sunday , gambling. Frequent complaint's had reached him, and he had sent mit constables attired in private clothes to catch offen- ders. Thu- punishment meted out to them however had not as yet. apparently effected the desired improvement. and he howd the Bench would make an example of these hovv.—St,vens, Robinson, Ball and Nield, who had been previnitsly convicted were fined 10s. including costs and the remaining defendants ss. including costs, each to he incarcerated for seven days in the event of non- payment.

DAMAGE TO OATS.—James Glee ve, Warringten, was charged with having on the 13th tilt. at Warrington, malicioinily damaged and destroyed some roots, the pro- perty of Win. Owen, and doing injury to the extent of £l. Mr. Browne, who represented the complainant, stated that his client was a hay and milk dealer in Bank- st„ and he tenanted the fields belonging to the Ship Canal Company at Arpley, which were surrounded by the river diversion and the river. On the date in ques- tion the complainant saw Mr.Gleaye break through one of his fences and walk through a field of oats., The oats were about two feet Lligh, and they received consider- able damage. Mr. Owen went to the defendant and re- minded him that be had previously warned him about trespassing on his land. A letter was sent to the defend- ant but he had taken no notice of it. Mr. Wm. Owen and Mr. Joseph Harrison each deposed to seeing the de- fendant walking across a field of oats. They considered the amount of damage to be at least £l. For the defence it was contended by the defeaciant that no damage had been done, and that ,previously there was an old towing path which led to the field. Finding that this had been stopped, he wa!lc,d across the field to save him going pack. Me. Weir. a witness, considered that the damage done was not above ss. The magistrates ordered the defendant to pay 10s. damage and costs. The defend- ant on leaving the box called Mr.3rowne a pettifogging lawyer. Mr. Browne thereupon applied for a penalty. The magistrates allowed one guinea as advocate's fee. ASSAULT.—James Morrison, collier, Buttonwood, was charged with having on the 17th ult. at Buttonwood beaten and assaulted Martin Chuchill. Mr. Browne represented the complainant, and Mr. Davies defended. Mr. Browne stated (hat the two parties had been to the Pear Tree Inn, Burtonwoed, on flee date in qaestion and when the complainant was walking home, the defendant. who was accompanied by two other men, struck the complainant in the eye and knocked him to the ground. Whilst he was on the ground the defendant also kicked him in the face and chest. The man shouted for help, and soon afterwards a man named Davies Swallow came to his assi,tance. The complainant was taken home, and had been in bed suffering from the injuri,s he received, for a week. Dr. Valentine, of Eirlestown, had attended him. The complainant gave evidence as to the assault and denied that he had given the defendant any provocation. Davies Swallow, collier, Buttonwood, spoke as to going to the assistance of the complainant. He was bleeding a great deal in the face. Witness took him home. P.C. Grundy said he was called to the complainant's house on the 18th inst. The man was in bed and his face was much swollen. His face was cut and he also complained of injury to his chest. Mr. Davies for the defence contended that the defendant was provoked by the complainant's conduct. Soon after leaving the public-house the complainant came tc the defendant and called him a foul name. The complainant then " squared out "and struck the first blow. He, however, got the worst of it. He (Mr. Davies) contended that the defendant should be dis- missed as the complainant was the aggressor. Evidence in support of this statement was given by John Carrick and Michael King. Mrs. C. Jackson, Collins Green, also gave evidence for the defence. The magistrates imposed a fine of ss. and costs. •

" PITCH AND Toss."—Thomas Mallet, James Rass, Jag. Unsworth, and Patrick Mallet, all of GAborne, were charged with having on the 17th ult., at Golborne. played at a game of chance called 'Pitch and Toss." The police withdrew the ease against the first-named defendant,it being stated that he was an imbecile. The other defendants were fined Is. and costs.

NEGLECT OF FAwitY.---George Murphy was charged with neglecting his wife and family. Mrs. Murphy stated that an order was made by the magistrates on ,19th July, 11392, that the defendant should pay 104. per ; week to her maintenance. The defendant was £2O in arrears. 0 i the understanding that the defendant went tack to live with her, the complainant withdrew the summons. The defendant agreed to do so. WlT:tour A GUN LICENCE.=HEAVY FINE. William Litherhinta clerk,was charged with having on the 14th May, at Newton, unlawfully carried and used a gun without haying a gun licence. Defendant pleaded guilty. An excise officer stated that the defendant was seen by three witnesses 'shooting birds on a farm at Newton on the date named. The case was further aggravated by the defendant not haying, since the date of the off,rule,taken nut a licence. Defendant was fined 20s. and co•tg, the Chairman stating that he hoped that the case would he a cautinn to others.

CRUMLTY TO ANIMALS—Robert Howard, fish dealer, Southport. was charged with having on the 71h ult. cruelly illtreated and abused an animal by working it in iia.fit state. Inspector Luff, R.5.P.C..A., stated that he was at E irlestqwn on the date named, when he saw the defendant in charge of a grey mare attached to a finh cart. The animal was very lame. On the near fore ipa the animal was r,uffering from ringbonr, and on the off-fore leg there was spavin. The animal was com- pletely worn out. P.C.Barnescorroborated,and said the horse was in a wretched condition. Defendant was finea 101. and costs.—Tames La.ngford.Haydock, was charged with a sitnilar offoine to a horse,on the Btholt.,at New- ton. '.inspeetar Luff gave evidence as to seeing the de- fendant driving a mare attached to a waggonette. The house was lame, and suff.ring from ringbone. It was tob.lly unfit,. for work. div.head: WATi B I NGTON WALKING DAY.
div.p: WATi B I NGTON WALKING DAY.
THE PROCESSION.

The weather on Friday, on the occasion of the annual festival at Warrington, left nothing to be desired. At the commencement of the week the weather was very unprosmising,but during the past few days the sun has shone forth with great power, and yesterday not a single dark cloud appeared to raise any fears oi rain to spoil the day's enjoyment. • I The decoration of the streets of the town com- menced on Thursday night, when numerous flags were hung out of various places of business. On Friday morning the scene was very brilliant, the whole length of the lin3 of procession being be- decked with 'bunting,&e. The streets were already crowded by nine o'clock, and by the time of the commencement of the procession of the schools through the streets,the whole route was lined with spectators. The schools commenced to arrive at the plot of ground in • front of the Town Hall at about 9.30, coming in by the east gate past the school attendance inspector's office. At about 10.15 the procession filed out by the west gate headed by the Blue Coat school. The route taken was through Sankey-st., Arpley-st., Wilson Patten-st., past Arpley Station, Bridge-st., Buttermarket-st., Church-st., after which they separated to their various churches. The Blue Coat school was headed ny their brass band under the conductorship of Mr. Rose.. After them followed the Workhouse children, among others in the pro- cession being Messrs. W. Houghton, Heaton, Auk- land, A. Jolley, Shaw, Gill, Muir, Davies, Hill (members of the Board of Guardians), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), and C. H. Ward (workhouse master). The smaller children were upon a lurry lent by Mr. Heaton. The Padgate Industrial School children followed led by their brass band, and Mr. and Mrs. H. M. Mines. 'After these came the Parish Church school children headed by the South Lancashire Volunteer Band, and by the church lads' brigade in command of Captain Buckton. There were also in the procession the Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis), Mr. R. T. Fairciough, &c. A slight accident occurred while this school was going out of the park. Two hurries holding a number of the smaller children were going under the tree-4 when a large flag came in contact with a bough and was broken in two. Fortunately no'one was hurt. Bank-st. and George- sr. missions were headed by the Volunteer bugle band, and the children had a plentiful supply of union jacks. The Iloly Trinity Church followed with the Walton brass band at their head, and there were also in the procession the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Messrs. Beacon,thilton,Hatton,and Westbrook. St. Luke's Church scholars were in charge of the Rey. R Wild. St. James' Church, Latchford, who came next, were wii hout doubt the pick of the pro- cession. The banner was of the form of a shield. and looked very pretty and the band was that of the South Lancashire Volunteers. A .very conspic- uous feature of the procesztion of this school was the mail carts upon which children were drawn. The wheels were covered with daises, and above them were canopiea of art muslin of various colours. They made a very agreeable change to the proces- sion. St. Ann's Churcb'came next, and at the head of the prodession were the Rev. J. Davies, Messrs. H. Rigby,Baird and P. standall. The St. Barnabas Church was in chatge of the Rev. G. Alton, and beaded by Fletcher's and Russell's brass band. In St. Peter's Church School, which Was headed by the Revs. B. Percival and J. Cooil, mail carts covered with daisies were also prominent. The Emmanuer Church at the head of which was the Rev. E. T. Reed, was plentifully supplied with banners, and the rear was brought up by the Christian Endeav- our flag. Legh-street Primitive Methodist school were preceded by their own band, and the Rev. W. .J. Kirkland was also present, and they were fol- lowed by the Primitive Nlethodist Church of Latch- ford. Buckley-street also had their own band at their head, and the scholars looked very well- There was a large number of boys and girls in the Ragged school procession. and they were headed by their drum and fife band playing the usual air. "Onward Christian Soldiers.' They were followed by the Gospel Union sunday School who were sup- plied with a large number of very small flags. The rear was brought up by the Salvation Army with their band. They had a large number of young chileren they had picked up in the streets. The ptocession took altogether three quarters of an hour to pass by, so that it. is evident that there was an enormous number of children in the schools repre- sented. It is estimated that there was an increase of about 1,500 children on the previous year. After parading the town, a service was held in the Parish Church, when the Rev. G. B Thurston delivered an address. The Roman Catholics had a separate procession in which the schools of St. Albans Sr Mary's (Buttermarket- =treet) and St. Mary's, (Latchford) took part. There was a very good turn out, and the various Catholic elergy of the the town were also present. The Borough Brass Band headed the procession. A new banner of St. Alban had been painted and given by Mr. Joseph Richardson and was at a very prominent feature of the procession. The greater part of the Nonconformists left the town t or Frodsbatn and various other places. During the afternoon, the various schools dispersed to different fields, were they enjoyed themselves until a late hour. At St. Elphin's Park,sports were held during the afternoon We give the following details with reference to the various schools. BOLD-STREET WR4LEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Number of scholars on books, 253 malts, 248 females; number of teachers. 26 males, 24 females; number of books in library, 410; ministers. Rev. J. feirtlan, Owen Watkins, 0. D. Mason, J. Gunnell; superintendent, Mr. W. Silcock ; secretaries, Messrs. W. A. Mellor and F. T. Wilson; treasurer, Mr. 0. Weaver; librarians, Messrs. Dunn and Bodle. The day. was spent in a field belong- , ing to Mr. Done, at Keckwick. The scholars journeying • by train to Darestairy. SILVER-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Number , of scholars on books, boys 200, girls 210; average attendance, bays 130, girls 174; number of teachers, 43 ; number of books in library, 440 ; ministers, Rev. J. Kiitlan, Rev. Owen Watkins and Rev. G. D. Mason; superintendents, Councillor J. S Green, J. W. Hayward, J.P. At 9 o'clock the scholars proceeded down Tanners- lane. Freghall-lane, Crosfield-street, and Parker-street., for Bank Quay Station. From the station the children went by train to Helsby and spent the day in afield on , the side of Helsby Hill. Tea and dinner was provided for both scholars and friends.

ELLESMME-ST. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Number of scholars on books, bw:cs. 112 ; girls, 140; average at- tendance, boys, 74 ; !:dris, 110; number of teachers, 13 male, 9 female; ministers, Revs. J. Kirtlan, 0. Watkins, and G. D. Mason ; superintendents, Messrs. P. L. Richardson and. no. Ban 'a'• schtiliirs met at the schoolroom at 9 a.m. They formed in procession; and time edict to a field in Padgate which was kindly lent hy Mr. W. Bennett. The younger children were conveyed in lorries lent by Mr. J. Ernmis and Mr. Howard, The day was spent in the usual manner, and was brought to a close by the scholars singing opposite to the house of Mr. Bennett. WYCLiFFF. SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Num her of scholats on la!mits, 642; averoge attendance, 452; number of rw-lchers, 38 and 5 officers ; number of books in library, 300 ; .minister, Reit. John Yonge ; superintendent, Mr. George Wallington. The scholars assembled at the ! school at 9 o'cloek and left in time to catch a special train for Acton Budge at 10 o'clock from Bank Quay. Dinner and tea were provided and sports and caries were indulged in during the day. Prizes were given for racing. PARTICULAR BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, Lynn-ST.— • Number of scholars on books, boys, 40 ; girls, 52 ; aver- age attendance, boys, 30 ; girls,s2 ; number of teachers, males, 6 ; females, 3 ; ministers, various ; superinten- dent, Mr, John Lingard. The scholars proceeded to a field kindly lent by Mr. Gill. After indulging in games, and refreshments they proceeded to school at 6.30 for tea, and then returned to the field for the rest of the day. BRICK-ST. SUNDAY SCllooL.—Number of scholors on books, 140 boys, 110 girls ; average attendance, 120 boys, 100 girls ; nincbor of teachers. 14 male, 7 female; ministers, varicus,superintendents,Messrs.J. Gandy and Robert Henshall. The scholars started from Friars Green Chapel at 9 o'clock. They proceeded to Brick-st school where there were lurries waiting to convey the small children to Pad.o.te where a field had been placed at the disposal of the school by Mr. Bennett. div.head: WALKING DIY AT PENKETH.
div.p: WALKING DIY AT PENKETH.

Friday being Walking Day a general holiday was ob- served in the village. About 10 15 the Mission scholars assembled, and waited for the scholars from Sankey School to arrive when a start was made. ThP proces- sion looked very gay with its multitude of flags and banners • and special attention' was attracted by the Church Lads Brigade marching in their uniform. After parading the village they proceeded to the field where a lunch of buns and milk was served to t4e scholars. After lunch they disported on the ground until teatime. After tea the various sports were again commenced varied by races, jumping contests, Itc. The Wesleyan School also paraded the village as- sembling at the school at one o'clock. At 1.15 a start was made when the procession proceeded through the village until tea time. After tea the scholars trooped to the Recreation Groaind where various sports were indulged in. About 9 the scholars dispersed for home.

div.head: CORPORATE FINANCE.
div.p: CORPORATE FINANCE.

The annual meeting of the Institute of Borough reasurars and accountants was held th tother week in the Council Chamber at the Liverpool Town Hall. By a wise policy the Borough Treasurers invited to their conference the Mayor chairman and vice chairman of the Finance Committees of the various Boroughs whose trea- surers are members. The assembly on Thursday and Friday was remarkable in several ways. First by the presence of so many mayors and also by the character of the papers read before the members. Acting on the suggestion of the secretary of the In- stitute the Warrington Finance Committee deputed his vice-chairman (Mr. Councillor Shaw Green) and Mr. Councillor Arthur Bennett to attend as a de- putation from this borough and accompanie.el by the mayor they attended the sittings of the Conference. Most important financial considerations were intro- duced by different members, the President taking up the subject of Corporation L tans showing that they had increased in sixteen years from ninety ; two millions to two hundred and one millions and calling attention to the very partial way in which theloa,ns were ordered to be repaid and giving his opinion further that the rate per bent which was the basis upon which the repayment was calcul- ated was altogether too high. Another subject discussed at length was the manner of dealing with unremunerative capital ex- penditure,the discussion being chiefly how to state the. expenditure in the accounts and whether such expenditure as sewering, draining,and street mak- ing should be considered assets. Another subject was the manner of 'setting out the general state- ment of the affairs of a borough or what account- ants commonly call the balance sheet. There was a remarkable 'diversity of opinion upon this, and it seemed impossible for the membew to arrive at.an unanimous decision, although it a ust be admitted that nothing can be more desirable than unanimity. The representative of Bolton (Mr. Swainson) had put his ideas in concrete form and produced a gene- ral statement,which he strongly advocated,dad had the other ideas been so worked out it would have appeared at sight which best expressed the general opinion. Another important matter 'referred to by the President was the audit of corporate accounts. The present manner of audit he declared must soon come to an end, and he showed the possibility of the Local Government Board endeavouring to se- cure them for their own auditors. Many members of the institute were, however, ot the opinion that this was a subject that ought not to pass out of the hands of the professional auditors, such as the members of the Institute of the Society of Account- ants. Paperseipon separate parishes, main and contri- butory roads, income tax assessments borrowing powers, &c.. filled up the time of the con f-rence and it was felt at the close that a very subs.utial amount of influence had been obtained .on .the whole.

To the Warrington deputation the various matters were partly interesting as it is well understood the Corporation is about to make some important finan- cial alterations and every particle of information that could be of service was eagerly sought fon by its treasurer and the representatives. A very brilliant gathering at am" at home "by the Lord Mayor added much to the enjoyment of the proceedings.

div.head: ENCOURAGING REPORT.
div.p: ENCOURAGING REPORT.

On Tuesday evening, the monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Town Hall, _Runcorn, Mr. Joseph Pritchard presiding. There were also present the Revs. Canon Maitland Wood, and Dr. Gastaldi„ Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Handley, J.P., E. Imison and G. Moss clerl:. GREENWAY-ROAD EVENING CONTINUATION CLASSES. At a meeting of the School Management Committee on the 20th ult. a report from the Education Department on the work done during the past session at the above school wan read by the Clerk. It stated that the amount of the grant was £7O 17s. 6d. which sum with other revenues. left a balance to be carried forward to next year. The Inspector's remarks as shown in the sum- mary were that the boys department continued to do excellent work, and was conducted with marked zeal, energy, and intelligence. The girls' department has made a promising start under Miss Kilburn, needlework being particularly well taught. The committee consid- ered these remarks to be very gratifying, and the report on the whole was highly satisfactory.—The minutes were confirmed by the Board, on the proposition of Dr. McDougall. SCEIOOL ATTENDANCE COWHITTEE.

This committee held a meeting on the 12th of June and considered the sums which the parents of blind and deaf children should pay them for the maintenapce of their children in institutions specially adapted for their instruction. The parents of children who had been sent to school by the Board were present at the meeting,.and after an exhaustive enquiry into the circumstances of the families, the committee decided to recommend that the Board agree to accept from Thomas Thompson, Suffolk-street', 23. per week; and is. 6d. per week from George Ramsden, Back Mersey-street. At a meeting on tb3 26th June the visitors reports were read showing that the number of scholars on the rol:s was 3,420, against 3,636 in June of last year, making a decrease of 216. The average attendar.ce was 2,934 compared with 3.061 in the corresponding period of the previous year, thus showing a decrease of 127. The percentage was 851, against 84.2 twelve months ago. The Clerk observed that the percentage was the high- est that had ever been reached. Dr. Gastaldi proposed and Mr. Handley seconded the confirmation of the minutes whichwere carried. A NEW MULJECT OF INSTRUCTION IN SCHOOLS. A circular letter was read from Lord Termaletown in which he urged the Board to consider the desirability of making compulsory the teaching in Board Schools of the effects and nature of alcohol upon the human system. The letter was referred to the School Management Committee for consideration. THE UNION OF LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE INSTITUTES. The Clerk reported the receipt of a communication from this Institute asking for the names of the repre- sentatives appointed to attend the fortheorning confer- ence.—lt was at length decided that Mr. Irni&ai and the Clerk should represent the Board at the meeting. TENDER.

The tender of Mrs. Tonks, Lord-st., for whitewashing and painting the Mid Brow and Greenway-road Board Schools was accepted. THE NEW CARETAIZEit OF THE GREENWAY-ROAD SCHOOLS. The School Management Committee met , previous to the Board meeting for the purpose of apyinting a care- taker for the Greenwa,y-road Board Schools and at length decided upon Mr. A. J. Keys, of Chestrr, as the successor. There were thirty applications.

div.head: TILE WORK OF A CORONER. INTERESTING STATEMENT BY MR. BRIGHOUSE. .
div.p: TILE WORK OF A CORONER. INTERESTING STATEMENT BY MR. BRIGHOUSE. .

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on Tuesday at the Parade-room of the Warrington police station upon the body of Alice Mary Win- stanley, aged four years, who died on the oreceding Friday from injuries received from a fall. The in- quest bed bean fixed for Monday afternoon, but after the jury had met together, a telephonic mes- sage was received from Mr. Brighouse saying that he found it impossible to be present owing to the length of time it took a jury to egret at West _ _
Derby. Mary Elizabeth Winstanley, the mother of the de- ceased said that she resided at Walker,:t. On Tuesday the 19th of last month, her daughter went upstairs to

bring a doll carriage down, and tell down three steps. She did sot appear to suffer much from the fall tor she got up herself and nothing more was thought about it. Two days afterwards she went to see her grandmother, and on coming back the said that she had bumped her head against a lamp-poet. There was a bruise upon the temple where she had been hurt, and in the evening, she became poorly. She grew so much .worse on the Saturday, that Dr. Adams was sent for. On the Tuesdny before her death, he became uncon- scious, and it was only at intervals that she recovered .consciousness. She died on Friday morning at 4.30. The Coroner read a letter from Dr. Adams stating that in his opinion the deceased died from inflammation o e the covering of the brain. The Coroner at this point said he was very sorry that he could not come the day betore. It was unavoidable or he would have been present. Mr. Thomas Smith, a juryman, said that he thought it was unjust that a man sheuld have to cerne from his work to attend the inquest after he had been there yesterday. He considered that the coroner was to blame. Mr. Brighouse asked Mr. Smith to be careful what he was saying. He always tried to accommodate the jury- men to the best of his power. To give Mr. Smith an :idea of what work he (Mr. Brighouse) had to do, be would tell him what he had done on the previous day, and it would then be seen that a coromer did not work on the eight hours system. On Monday he had to hold eight inquests in South West Lancashire. He lel; home at c-27 a.m. to hold an inquest at St. Helens Junctien at 9.15. He held another inquest at Wa,vertree Town Hall at eleven o'clock, and then at one at the George lintel, West Derby at 12.35. He had another at Tuebrook, West Derby at one o'clock, after which he intended to catch the 2.30 train to Warrington to bold the inquest at three o'clock. At the inquest at Tuebrook, however, there was one juryman who' would not agree with the other eleven. Lie (Mr. Brighouse) could not r..imnpel the man to do so, and the jury werekept together a dread- ful length of time—much longer than he anticipateci. He had to be at Flindley Green at 5.50 so therefore lie was compelled to let the Warrington inques-.. slide. He had another inquest at Ince near Wigan at 730, and finished up at Pemberton at 8.30. He arrived home at 10.30 p.m. and he had to get up at seven o'clock that morning to hold the inquest at Warrington. He would like t- have held the inquest the previous day if possible, as he could -very well have done with another hour or two at home that morning. He would ask Mr. Plinston, the foreman ,of the jury, whether-in les experience he (Mr Brig- 'house) had not done his best to prevent any inconveni- --once to the juries. • Mr. Piinston said that he had been on juries before Mr. Brighouse was appointed and frequently since, .and he always found him to be very obliging in every, Way. Inspector Bowen said that it frequently tack two hours to summons a jury, because the police never t:iok a man away from his business if possible. Mr. Smith said that he did not blame the police. The Coroner: I will not allow you to blame Me. He further went on to siv that in strict law, the police could summon 12 or any number to attend an inquest and they would be obliged to attend. lie was, however, anxious not to inconvenience anyone. • Mr. Smith expressed himself satisfilKi and the jury than returned a verdict of" Accidental death."
