div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The Warrington cricketers are getting on, for they have actually won their second victory. This wonderful result occurred at Arpley on Saturday, when the proud Prestonians had to tow the knee to the cricketers of the "good old town." It was a pity that there were not more present to witness this feat, for the game was a first class one. It was unfortunately for the exchequer of the club, trip day, aud therefore some fow thousands had left Warrington for some more salubrious spot. Tak- ing these facts into consideration, the" gate" was not a bad one. Warrington 'ere fortunate in winning the toss, which they took advantage of by going in to bat first.

The first two cricketers who went in were almost of themselves sufficient to knock a lot of the confidence out of the Preston men. These were S. M. Crosfield and Bates. These two seemed to be quite at home with the Preston bowling for they made twclve runs out of one over by Holmes. Needless to say this was too much and another bowler was put on. lie however, fared no bet- ter, in fact the Warrington batsmen were so impartial that they served all alike until lunch time came. This appeared to have a bad effect upon the batsmen, forsoon after coming to the wickets again, Bates put his left leg before a straight bill and was therefore obliged to go to the pavilion. He had scored an excellent 44,a.nd he and Crosfield together had put on 118 runs for the first wicket. With this good start, a record score ought to have been made, but no! George Clarke and R. Smith each walked to the wickets and walked back again with- out troubling the scorer at all. Then S.M. Crosfield hail to go after making 73 which ha did in 4 brilliant style. The procession was not yet finished for Callon, Glark, Bibby, Williamson, and Un3worth quickly followed, the only two remaining batsmen who were able to withstand the attack being Griffin who made 10 and Connor who carried out his bat for 17. The venture therefore real- ized 189 runs, a good score considering the "rot " which existed during the middle part of the innings.

The Prestonians did very badly at the commencement of their innings,for instead of getting 118 for one wicket like Warrington, they lost a raan before a run was scored This was owing to the prowess of Connor, whose day out it was on Saturday. This gentleman, who is,or was a member of the famous Preston North ,End football team, also showed that he Was as much at home with the cricket ball as with the footblll. He clean bowled six of the Prestonians, including the well-known " Jim-, my " Ross, and caught two other batsmen. His bowling Analysis with the six Wickets for 36 runs, 'arid the opinion has been expressed that he may be seen in the county before long, as a change bowler at the pres- ent time would be very acceptable. The highest contri- bution on the side of Preston was that of Punchard who made 33 not out, and well justified his name. S. M. Crosfield had not very much bowling but he succeeded in capturing one wicket for two runs. The Warring- toniaos were rather lax in the fielding, or otherwise the victory of 169 to 117 might have. been even more deci- sive.

To-day they meet Cheetham Hill for the .first time this season. Another victory should be the result, but so erratic are the doings of the team that it would be diffi- cult to say what they will do. 'They appear to have a " weakness" for taking down big teams as witness the show they made against Manchester, Preston and Sefton, but when the team has not such an imposing name, they do not do themselves credit. However, let U 3 hope that they will send the representatives of the Palestine of Manchester back with something to moralise over.

The Warrington second were unable to come 1.113 to the first team, tor they were beaten by Winnington Park by 94 to 62. Whatever were the Warrington team doing to adow their opponents to score 17 extras out of 94 runs? This had a great deal to do with the victory of Winnington Park, for there is not so very much between the two teams when this is left' out.

Sankey Bridges team, assisted by two or three other players, were not equal to the task of overcoming the Welshmen of Llandudno. When a man scores 133 alone and another 64 not out, it makes things look rather bad for the other side. Llandudno were fortunate to win the toss, and so harmless was the bowling they had to fdce that 255 runs were scored for the lose of only two wickets. Against this score Sankey Bridges were able to make in, Clarke taking nine of their wickets. The chief scorers for the visitors were Bearnau with 36, Bailey with 30 and Peers pith 15. Although the visitors had ;A: had time of it on the Ilea:, they had a good time aft, r wards, for they thoroughly enjoyed theinselves,and are lookirag forvvar..l to another visit next year.

The C.L.C. Engiueera went to Birkenhead to meet the C.L.C. of that town on Saturday, arid came hack with the pleasure of having won a victory by 57 to 32. For Vie Warrington team Shaw obtaineo 27 and S. Howard 14. Lawlecs had a hand in the distnipal of seven of the Birkenhead ba.tsrncn.

The two teams whose names are so lornbre, the Ceme- tery White Rose, and the Cemetery Jtini6rs could not settle their differences on Saturday, atttion.2h the Juniors almost won. The White Rose were all out for 39, and the Juniors had come within four runi of this number for the IOSS Of 011;57 two Wickets when time iN as up, and the match was a draw. Ffard lines for the Juniors.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
EXTRAORDINARY YACHTING DISASTER.

The yachting on the Clyde on Thursday was m3rred by an extraordinary disaster. Many boats crowded the water for those on board to see the start for the Muir Memorial Cup race. It is said that the competing yachts had not, consequently, room enough to tack. Anyhow the Satanita crashed into the Valkyrie amidships, and cut her down to the water's edge. The Valkyrie's cabin filled, and she sank in a few minutes. Lord Dunraven, his guests, and crew were rescued by the boats lying at the starting-point. One of the men on board the Val- kyrie was seriously injured.

div.head: ATTERCLIF.Fz. ELECTION.
div.p: THE ATTERCLIF.Fz. ELECTION.

The Attercliffe election (one of the divisions of She- ffield) resulted on Thursday in the return of Alderman Batty Langley, the Liberal candidate, by a majority of 991. over Mr. Hill Smith, the Tory. Mr. Frank Smith, the Independent Labour candidate, polled 1,249 votes. Altouethi.r 9.230 voters recorded their votes. The constituency numbers 11,696, but its actual voting strength, owing to removals and other causes, is about 10,250. There was thus a good poll.

The" Daily News "says there is only one thing to be said about this result. It is simply splendid. It is a straight-forward thorough-going vote of confidence in the Government froth a constituency as thoroughly representative of the working classes as any in the United Kingdom. It shows that, while Independent Labour is a force with which we must reckon, Toryism is nowhere among the masses. Mr. Hill Smith fought with every conceivable advantage in his favour. He had stood before and had reduced Mr. Coleridge's majority. He had against him a.divided,in place of a united party. He had on his side wealth, prejudice and pressure. Mr. Langley was roundly and ignorantly abused by a great many people who knew nothing about his but who thought it was democratic " business" to rail at him. We congratulats Mr. Langley upon his courage and the Liberal Association of AtterclifTe upon understanding what they were about. They chose the right man, they stuck to him, and they have returned him with a more than decisive preponderance. Mr. Frank Smith has done well. But the Tory,or rather perhaps the Dissentient Liberal alliance with independent Labour, has been smitten under the fifth rib.

' The "Times" says —There is the broad fact that in a contest which called but a small number of new electors into action the Labour candidate has withdrawn close upon 1,100 votes from the regular party organisations. This is the more noteworthy because Mr. Pickard, speaking with all the authority of centralised trade unionism, did his best to persuade and almost to com- mand working-men to give their undivided support to the Gladstonian candidate. But for his action, it is natural to assume, the losses of the Gladstonian party would have been much heavier than they are. This is one of the most striking proofs yet laid before the public of the growth of a third party standing aloof from the two great groups which have so long managed the affairs of this' country as to make it bard for some minds to coneeive any other arrangement. It is true that the Labour party has not even now returned its nominee,but it has shown a vitality all the more remarkable becauie there is no suspicion of coddling. Mr. Ftank Smith's very considerable success, won in the teeth of opposition from the working-class organisations which ought to have aided him, is evidence of the growth among the rank and file of feelings with which trade union leaders will ere long have to reckon.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday evening, the Queen's reply to the address of the House or the occas- ion of the assassination of M. Carnot was read. Her MAJESTY said she would convey to the French Govern- ment the abhorrence which, in common with herself. the House felt at this detestable crime and the sympathy which it had called forth for the family of the late President and also for the Government and people of France. The House again went into Committee on the Budget Bill. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT moved a clause granting an exception in regard to the estate duty in favour of property in the colonies subject to,duty there, and after some discussion the clause was agrlvd to. Divisions took place on several Conservative amend- ments. resulting in their defeat by majorities of between 50 and 60. The bill passed through Committee at 10.15 and was reported. ' It was afterwards recommitted in respect of clause 27, relating to the spirit duty, and Mr. CLANCY moved the rejection of the clause. Mr. W. Ilcumono supported this motion. On a division the clause was carried'by 198 to 185, and the Committee stage of the hill WIS thus finally completed. The report stage was fixed for Monday next.

div.head: TilE LOCAL FBJENDLY SOCIETY'S ACTION.
div.p: TilE LOCAL FBJENDLY SOCIETY'S ACTION.
ADJOURNED HEARING.

Before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes at the Warringpon County Court on Thursday, the adjourned hearing of the action by Messrs. Tunst,all and others, trustees ot the Ashton-in-Makerfield district of the Independent Order of Odc.fellows- Manchester Unity Friendly Society, against John Butter. field and his son John James Tatham Butterfield,was held Mr. Cobbett. of Messrs. Cobbett, Wheeler and Cobbett. solicitors, Manchester, represented the pla,intiffs, and Mr. Allen (Messrs. Peace and Ellis, solicitors, Wigan) appeared on behalf of the lessors (Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Ltd) The defendants were unrepresented. The application of the plaintiff's was that his Honour would give them a declaration that the younger defend- ant, John James Ta•liam Butterfield, was a trustee of the land and lease for his father in respect of a plot of land at the corner of Athol-street, and Portland-street, Earlestown, ot which Messrs. R. Evans and Co.. Ltd., were the lessors, and the plaintiffs also desired that the land should be vested in the senior defendant, John Butterfield, or the plaintiffs, or such other person as the court might direct. His Honour at the last sitting of the court made the declaration, that the son was the trustee of the land and lease for his father, and the adjournment was made in order to hear the second part of the application. Mr. Allen applied for a further adjournment of the proceedings as the lessors had had no notice of the pro- ceedings.—His Honour said he was quite agreed that the lessors ought to have had notice.—Mr. Cobbett con- tended that Mr. Allon's clients were not 'a party in the action.—His Honour said he could not adjourn the case. Mr. Cobbett said he desired an order vesting the land in Butterfield, senior, and a foreclosure order, which was subject to costs, but which was merely a consequential matter. They were trying to undo what the senior de- tendant had wrongly dove.—His Honour: I don't think I should be asked to undo a fraud.—Mr. Cobbett con- tended that one of the principal objects of law courts was to put right frauds. The moment his Honour made a foreclosure arder it would have the effect of entitling the plaintiffs at a proper date to "enforce their security,so that the senior defendant would not have the benefit of the fraud. His Honour was being asked to assist innocent persona to put right a wrong. It was not as if Butterfield could obtain one iota of benefit from those proceedings.—His Honour said he thought the plaintiffs were entitled to foreclosure, but why did they want a vesting order when they were the equitable mortgagees?-4;„ Cobbett said what the plaintiffs asked for was, that they might be in the position; that within' six months, if Butterfield senior had not paid them off, they might be entitled to lay claim to this property. If he (Mr. Cobbett) could see that any injury legal or moral could accrue to any person by the order he was asking for, he. would not persist in the view he was taking. He could not see but that good would be the restilt of it. His Honour would be helping a society of poor working people to reccver meney they had .parted with. He therefore asked his Honour to vest Ellis term in Butterfield senior, and that he make the foreclosing order, leaving them to add costs to their security.—His Honour said he did not feel disposed to decide the case that day, so far as a vesting order was concerned. He did not see any reason why the plaintiffs ought not to be entitled to the order of foreclosure, because it was shown that they were the equitable mortgagees by the deposited lease of the land, aud•they did not seem by the evidence to have been in any way acquainted with the fraudulent prac- tices of the two Butterfields. They seemed to have acted in good faith on the strength of the security offered. He would reserve his decision as to making a vesting order until next court day. An order for foreclosure would be granted, and the interest and costs allowed.

div.head: ST. HELENS
div.p: ST. HELENS
NNW INSTRUMENTS' FOR §CITTON BRASS BAND.

On Saturday, Messrs. Boosey and Son, of Landon, musical instrument manufacturers, delivered a new set of instrumentv to the Sutton-road Brass Band, St. Helens. The cost has beed £325. The Sutton Band was established in September, 1890, and since its forma- tion the members have shown a great- amount of deter- mination to excel. They are now in a position to successfully take part in contests, -which ha S beep their ambition for some time. The instruments are on view in the windows of the busirwss establishment of Coun- cillor Charles Walsh, the president of the band.

div.head: rap. EFFECTS OF LABOUR STRIKES.
div.p: rap. EFFECTS OF LABOUR STRIKES.

At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Mr!J. P. Mearns applied to Judge Shand, on behalf of Henry Bridge, a plumber, who also bad a grocery bu siness now of ilorougb-road. Some time ago' to increase his earnings,he purchased a business which was represented to turn over £lB to, £2O a week.. The bottlemakers' strike and the c,?al strike had ruined him, and he had sickness and other troubles. He bad £7O or £BO of bad debts: An offer to pay 108. in the pound was made,but his Honour considered the full 203. in the pound should be paid, and the case was adjourned for a month to see what applicant could arrange to do.

div.head: CORPORATION AND RAILWAY RATES.
div.p: THE CORPORATION AND RAILWAY RATES.

The Parliamentary committee of the St. Helens Cor- poration having considered a communication from the Secretary of the Mansion House Association on Railway' Rates, with respect to certain bills now before Parlia- ment.and also having considered the question of railway rates, have resolved chat in the interests of the trade of the country it is not only desirable, hut even necessary, that the legislation, particularly the Government bill al- ready introduced for the proLetion of traders in the matter of railway rates should be proceeded with and carried through during the present Session of Parlia- ment. The Town Clerk was instructed to forward a copy of the resolutionith the Chancellor of the Exchequer, to the President of the Board .of Trade, and to the borough .member. DkATR OF A WELL-KNOWN CONTRACTOR.

Mr. John Whittaker, f is7U't-tC;11,—ST.—I:1;;;;;,- a well- known local conttactor, died on Monday, after a few hours' illness. Mr. Whittaker came t6O St. Helens about forty years since, and in his earlier days was engaged in erecting, some of the high chimneys and glass works in the borough. Among the many contracts he took was the new baths in Boundary-road for the St. Helens Corporation, and included in the work he had in hand at the time of his death was • the new Palish Church schools for the vicar and wardens of St. Helens. and the -renovation of the St. Helena Parish Church, which was commenced on Monday. He was a well-known figure in the locality. Deeed,.who was advanced in years, leaves a widow aad a son.

ATTEMPTED SI7:CIDE. At S. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a respectable young fellow named William Sliiw, of Edison-square, Thatto Heath, was brought before Mr. A. Walmsl- Cotham on a charge of attempting to commit sttieid.e. Chief Constable, Wood raid the pris-pier was a ewer. On Saturday he had neen drinking, and about ten minutes to riine.on •Siinctly night he W4S,found by a man named William Jones liatiOng by the neck with a strap which WaS attached to a rafter. Jones got the assistance of anor.n,r man named..Martiodsle, and they unfastened the strip. SIAW was taken into the house, being nearly unc,ms:•,ious. Mr. Brighouseocoianty coroner, held an inqii;est at the Wheatsheat Hoiel, St. *Helens Junction, on Monday, on the body of George Clark, a day wage man at the Bold C,lhery, who lived in Pye•street, but who was killed by an express train on the main line of the London and. North-Western Railway between Liverpool and Manches- ter. Mr. Fenna represented the railway company. James Butler, a youth, vhci Wa.4 with deceased when he was killed, said they had (Aimed over the "sleeper" fencing on to the line. When the train passed them witness was blown to one side with the current,—James Shaw said he was in charge of the eight o'clock express from Liver- pool to Manchester on Thursday night. After he had passed St. Helens Junction Station he saw two men I walking, on the edge of the sleepers. He opened his whistle and 'kept it ging continuously until deceased was struck. Witness tried to stop the engine,but could not, because -he was going at the rate of fifty miles an hour.—A Juryman said a crowd of people were attracted to the line by the whistling of the engine.—Mr. Fenn* : said that on that portion of the line they had the great- est difficulty with trespassers. They had had a number • of convictions, and officers had been engaged to keep men oil% Ingnediati-ly the officers were out of .the way they flocked on the line in droves. There was a foot bridge, but the men did not use it, preferring to take a nearer cut from their work.. Time company. had spared neither trouble nor expense to make the fencing safe,but it .was being continually broken down. In one caso in which a Man was prosecuted the man had actually his hat; blown off by a passing train while struggling with the d-tectite.—Mr. James Lucas, station master at St. Helens Junction, gave evidence as to the finding of the men, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," attaching no blame to anyone. .

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

The annual trip given by Mr. T. Molyneux, to the children attending the various schools in the dis- trict, took place on Thursday to New Brighton. For several years past Mr. Molyneux has organised this trip, which he has given with the object of encour- aging regular attendance on the part of the children at chools, and only those scholars who have not been absent on a single occasion during the year were entitled to participate. Invitations were accordingly issued to 625 scholars,79 schoolmasters, mistresses, teachers and managers. In addition to these 75 parents and friends accompanied 'the chil- dren.. At an early hour the children were seen making their way to the various schools, where they marshalled in processional order, and marched to the station. A special train had been engaged, which with its human freight left Earlekown for Liverpool at 8.20. On arrival at Lime-street, the children walked in procession across the town to the landing stage, where they embarked on one of the ferry boats and sailed to New Brighton, where they arrived soon after 10 o'clock. They were not long in dispersing themselves over the sands and at noon aasenibled in the Palace for dinner. Tea was served at 5 o'clock, and after an exceedingly enjoyable day, they left for home 'about 6 o'clock, reaching Earlestown about 7.45 without mishap.

div.head: NEWTON BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT COIMISSIONEI.
div.p: NEWTON BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT COIMISSIONEI.

A meeting of this body was held at the Town Bali, Eltirlestown, on Monday afternoon. There were present:—Mr. J. W.Emmett (chairman),Messrs. T. Fenster, T. Ormand, E. T. Evans, G. Ratcliffe, P. McMahon, P. Thompson and J. Smith, Mr. Worsley (law clerk), and Mr. Brierley (clerk and surveyor). A letter was read from Col. McCorquodale regret:ing his inability to be present.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of tt.kis committee on the 18th ult., ten- ders for supply of cannel and coals for all purposes were submitted trotn various firms. Al ter some consideration and tests made by the gas manager, it was resOlved that the whole of the coal requirements be offered to Messrs. R. Evans and Co., Ltd., for the year ending June 30, 1895. It was further resolved that. the Chairman and Mr. Ormand be a special committee to settlethe contract for cannel, after tests to be made by the gas manager, and also as to bolts and other requirements at the gas works contained in the manager's report read at the meeting. , It was decided that the price of gas coke be advanced to 9s. per ton at the works, on and after the 25th inst., until further notice. The carbonizing account for the past month was read, giving fuel used 208 tons, 8 cwts. gas made 2,097,3001 t., being an average of 10,0531 t. per ton ,of fuel used. Tein minutes *ere passed. The Chairman said the sub-committee had decided, after tsts by Mr. Swann, to give the cannel contract to the White- cross Company for the ensuing year.

div.head: PUBLIC- WORKS AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: PUBLIC- WORKS AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.

At the meeting of this committee, Mr. Briertey read correspondence with Messrs. Leach and R. Davies and Co.' respecting ,the night-soil contract with the late Mr. W. Chambers, and the Law Clerk was instrutted to acknowledge Messrs. R. Davies and Co.'s letter and state that the committee awaited the trustees' suggestions. The committee resolved that in the construction of the schedule of fees and payment at the Cemetery, the term tombstone or monument was to include a headstone which was over the height of five feet. Mr. Gregory's report was read calling attention to the increased wOrk in the night-soil department and asking for some relief therefrom. It was decided that a person be appointed to take charge of the horses and night work at a weekly wage of 255., he being responsible for the proper condi- tion of the horses, carts, gears, and stables, and to the night workmen fulfilling their respective .duties. It was fu.rther resolved that an additional horse and cart be obtained for the night-soil work. A letter of the 23rd Ult., with a plan, from Messrs. R. Evans and Co., of pro- posed diversion of footpath, west of Crow-lane, for building purposes was considered, and it was resolved that they be informed that the committee had no objec- tion to the proposed diversion on the understanding that the cempany maintain the road in proper condition and comply with the requisite local formalities. The following plans were submitted and approved: Fourteen cottages in Clarence-street for Mr. G. Findley; two cottages in St. Helens-road for Mr. R. Leylandiand an amended plan of buildings. north of Crow-lane, for Messrs. It. Evans and Co:, Ltd. The minutes were passed without comment.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Chairman of this Committee reported the commit- tee's interview with Mr. Itich respecting the por,tal -arrangements at Earlestown and their requirements at the meeting ot the committee on the Bth ult. It was resolved that the special committee be requested to continue to urze for better accommodation and more suitable premises. The application of the local auditors for .consideration of their remuneration, for the extra duties performed by them, was before the committee and it was resolved that they be allowed £lO each for the past audit. . Accounts were submitted and cheques signed for payment amounting t(i £1,639 Is. 3d. The cominittee's minutes were approved of.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AND TECHNICAL INSTRUC TION COMMITTER.

The School Attendance Officer (Mr. Ball) read his report to a meeting of this Committee held on June 18, which was adopted. Mr. Ball was instructed to report to the Committee any future interference by Dr. Wat- kins with labour certificates. A form of particulais issued by the Technical Instruction Committee of the County Council was considered and it was explained by the secretary of the local committee (Mr. OrmaDid) when it was agreed to recommend an applita.tion to the County Council for a grant of £230 for the forthcoming session. The Committee further recommended •a grant ,of £BO from the CommissionerS June imprayement rate on account of the exp!nses of the Viaduct Technical .In- struction Committee for 1394-5. These minutes were pa-Jsed.

div.head: NEWTON DEPUTATION TO MR. RION.
div.p: THE NEWTON DEPUTATION TO MR. RION.

Mr. Emmett said he thought he ought to make a state- ment with regard to the deputation from gewton ,to Mr. Rich. Postmaster, Liverpool. The statements Made by the deputation, if they were correctly reported in the "Earlestown and Newton Examiner," were in his judg- ment inaccurate in two matters. The first was that there was no representative for Newton on that Board. That was not correct. There were Colonel McOorquo- dale, and Mr. Smith, two very good representatives for Newton. The other inaccurate statement was that the new buildings erected were all going " Newton wards." If they called the top of Market-st. in the direction of Newton, he was unable to understand them. le just simply made that statement as he thought the remarks of the Newton deputation 4eserved correction.

ANOTHER. PILLAR BOX FOR BARLBSTOWN. A communication front Mr. Jordan, postmaster for Newton, was read in which he asked the Commissioners to erect a oilbr box in Crow-lane near Pomona-terrace. It was decidPd on the motion of Mr. McMahon, seconded by Mr. Ti”.bninson, that .the work be carried out by the ComtniF•sioner6, the cost to be defrayed by the postal authorities.

THE NEXT MEETING OF THE BOARD. Ormand moved and Mr. Smith seconded that the next meeting, of the Board be held the second Monday in Atigtßt owing to bank holiday being the lirA Monday in the month.—The Chairman eave formal notice that he would propose the reappointment of Dr. Watkins as medical officer for the Board at the next meeting. This was all the business.

div.p: LYMM,

THE LOCAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting. of the Board tot,k place on Tuesday evening, when there were present—Mr. James Greeson (chairman), Messrs. R. Whiteleg.e, J. Holt, W, Braz-ndale.J. Perrin, E. Holt, and H. Harrison ; Ridgway (law Clerk), Mullard (clerk), Mort (surveyor). Severs (gas manager), and Rowe (cap- tain orthe fire brigade).—The Surveyor and Captain of the Fire Brigade submitted their reports, which con- tained no item of public interest. Mr. Severs, in .his report, stated that the production of gas during the past month had been 641,500 cubic feet, against 588,300' cubic feet for the corresp..nding period of the previous year, being an increase of 53,200 cubic feet. A RuisawaY FIORSIC—On iklonday, 'while the driver of a horse and trap belemging to Messrs. Fairclough and Sons, millers, Warrington, was in the Post Office at Heatley.transacting some business, his horse,which was a very spirited one, and was attached to a trap, took fright, and, although a weight was attached to if head, bolted down the road. The crossing gates at'.Heatley Station were shut to real traffic, and the sprang over, breaking a shaft, injuring itself slightly, and also doing damage to the workings of the gates. The animal was only extricated alter some trouble and with the as- sistance ot the railway officials.
ANNUAL ExcULISION OF MESSRS. GOSSAGE'S WOHKPEOPLE.

The annual excursion of the workpeeple, employed by Messrs W. Gossage and Sons, Limited, at the Widnes Soap Works, was held on Saturday. The employes were given the opportunity of choosing the place ta be visited and on a ballot being talt-in it was found that Llan- • dudno had been selected. Three lengthy trains left Widnes London and North-Western Station between 6.30 and 7 a.m. filled to their utmost capanity. Tim trains stopped at heveral plates in Wales including Rhyl, Colwyn Bay and Llandudno Junction and many persons brolo their journey at these places. At Llandudno a most enjoyable day was spent in visiting the planes of interest in and around the town. The return journey as commenced shortly after 6.30 p.m. and Widnes was reached in good time. The arrangements were carried out,.in an admirable manner and almost without excep- tion', worlrpeopl were most orderly and well! behard.
NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Haymaking was slightly interfered with by the storm and heavy downfall of rain on Monday, but very little, if any, damage was caused in consequence; and operations were resumed in some places the next day. Beneath the bridge in Wargrave Road the ground dips considerably and whenever there is a heavy fall of rain such as that which occurred on Monday, the road speedily be- comes flooded to the depth of two or three feet, rendering it impassable. There is certainly a grid on each side of the road, but they appear to be in- sufficient to take away the large volume of water, which rushes down each incline to the bridge. This state of things has been in existence now for many years, but no steps appear to be taken to remedy it. It certainly is high time some. alteration was made, but I suppose like everything else, the improve- ment must be brought ablut slowly and with deli- beration. Perhaps when we are divided into wards, and get 9ur own repres.enta'Aves, we shall have a better chance.

Visitors to Newton Common last Sunday would be struck with the quiet aspect of the surround- ings, when they considered that the day was popu- larly known as Race Sunday. Many will remem- ber the condition of things which existed about 12 years ago, when the neighbourhood of the race course wore something like the appearance of a fair Merry-go-rounds, shooting galleries, aunt sallies, and other forms of amusement were in full swing during the whole of Sunday, and the Sabbath was otherwise descrated. The spread of civilisation has however altered all this., and now we have no fear of the minds of our young people being demoralised by such "goings on." he action to put a stop to 31.1.1 h a state of things was not taken away too soon arid I sure the community are title gainers by its abolition.

The Medical Aid Society have every reason to feel grateful at the success which has attended the step 'they took in establishing a trained sick nurse in the district She has now been on duty three months and during that time has attended about 540 cases, and of course may be considered to have alleviated a proportionate amount of suffer- ing. I hope the necessity to dispense with her ser- vices will never arise, but it, of course, all depends upon the extent of public support the society receives. This Must he my excuse for asking the Cycling Club what steps they are taking to push forward the lantern parade. I learn that they have the matter under consideration, but they must have public support and sympathy, and a determination on all sides to support a,cause which is acknow- ledged to have so far been of inestimable benefit.

div.head: "OWD tPATRICROFT FER EVER!"
div.p: "OWD tPATRICROFT FER EVER!"

Aw like Owd Patricroft, becoze' ' Hoo's a Borough neaw, full blown, Wi' a fost-rate Mayor an' Ceauncillors, That's not excelled by noan. It's true, aw've seen um lookin' black, An' even feelin' But start a joke an' in a crack Thay're "meek an' mild ! " Aw like Owd Patricroft, becoze— We're wed l off fer a Vicar, Wo wudn't rob his meanest foes, 0' what thay like i' liquor. ile duz ez he'd be done unto,— • Don't beaunce that he's teetotal; An' never thinks to ovverdo Things sacerdotal) , Aw like Owd Patricroft, becoze Her footpaths are so narrow, Yo'ite ev'ry chance to get yer toes Crusli'd wi a huckster's barrow. • Or coorse, we cuiliet ax th' Police To regiailate this traffic; Their duty is to keep the peace, An' look seraphic! Aw like Owd Patricroft, becoze Her " Bobbies" are so tender, That if a woman geet to blows, Noon on urn la ud offend her. Surnames " Peggy Mason "street, Thay'll sheaut an feyght like blazes, An' even on a Sunday .neet, Sing owt but praises ! Aw like Owd Patricroft, becoze Its cheery, fer a change, Fro wheer thay never get to blows, • An' rows are reckon% strange. Aw'm noan that breed ez likes to see - • A' Peeler" i' distress.; Aw'd sooner her tarn watchin' • Than in a mess! Aw'm preaud o' Patricroft becoze, Her workheause is so grand ; 'An' when its finished, aw propose Its (ippon% wi' a band Thoose splendid gates mun oppen wide, An' gie us lots o' room;. Per nob'dy knows wot may hetideg Nor wot's his doom 1 . Aw'm preaud o' Patricroft becoze O'th' Auditors hoo's gEtten ; Who drop deawn on eaur Ceauncillors, An' wet thay'n drunk au' etten. Ov coorse, they do ther work fer nowt ; An' scorn to finger pay ; An' this is heaw it cuinsahout, • Thay've room to BRAY ! Aw like Owd Patricroft, becoze Bowlin' Greens galore, 11' parsons' beauses built quite close, Per th' Saints to look uz o'er! Its aw quite reet, fer don't yo see, A Bow•-,tr never swears; An' so it leaves the Clargy free To say ther prayers! Aw like Owd Patricroft, becoze Aw've chums i' ey'ry street, An' th' hardest jab aw hey to do, Is wishin' urn good fleet !. . • But eh, lads! heaw nay fiugerS aches, , Ther gettin' aw o'er segs ; So aw'll shut up, fer aw yer sakes.— Yore', 0' PEGS. Rose Bonk, July 4, 1891. •

div.head: RAILWAYS AND THE STRIKE.
div.p: THE RAILWAYS AND THE STRIKE.

The ScottiAi /,%liners' Federation have drafted a mani- festo to be sent to all tra le unions'in the kingdom explaining the eircumstinces of the strike and appealing for support. The stoppage of outpnt has already had considerable effect on the Scotch railways. Owing to the diminution of mineral traffic nearly two hundred locomotive engines have been placed in the sheds. No fewer than seveu hundred railway servants have been dismissed. AID FOR THE SCOTCH MINERS. THE PROTECTION OF LABOUR. •

A meetinr, of the Ececutive Committee of the Miners of Great Britain was held in Birmingham on Tuesday, 'Mr. Pickard presiding. It was decided to increase the levy in suppoit of the Scotch miners from 6rl-. to Is. A letter was received from the Durham Miners' Associa- ' tiation asking that a national conference should he ar- ranged to endeavour to tix upon a national policy for the protection of labour. .It was resolved to hold such a conference at Newcastle-on Tyne on the 12th inst.,and t. 3 invite all the coal districts in the kin.doin to attend. No communication was made as to further negotiations I with coalowners. '

THE ADJOURNED MEETING OF COALOWNERS. The adjourned meeting of the Coal Conciliation Board was held at St. Martin's Town Hall on Tuesday. Only the coalowners' representatives on the board were present, the miners' representatives having refused to attend, on the ground that the meeting was informally summoned„ Mr. A. M. Chambers presided, and the pro- ceedings were of a very brief character. Of the original members of the board, Mr. Williamson (Cannock Chase), Mr. Henry Dennis (North Wales), arm Messrs. Kellett and Johnson (Lancashire) were absent. Mr. Pilkington (Lanchashire) and Captain Harrison (Cannock) were present. On the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. Hewlett, the meeting adjourned until Saturday at noon. No further information was given to the Press, but it was understood that certain propositions were conveyed to the Miners' Federation Board.

Father - Clarke, • and Messrs. .J. W• Wareing, B. Brown, 8. Quinn, C. Flynn and G. IL. Da,nby (clerk). DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. , This Committee reported that (luring the month uf June (three weeks Nll free places were granted. TherP had also been 14 prosecutions before the magi6trares, of which there were 12 convictions and two sent to Truan:; School. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Father Clarke and Major Wareing. . CONTINUATION CLASSES. The following report of the evening continuation classes in connection with the West Bink Board Sehoel was read :—" Boys' School, Head Master Mr. Calland ; this school has been excellently conducted.
